entries.title: Deploy frontier AI models on AWS Trainium with SGLang-Neuron
entries.summary: SGLang-Neuron is now publicly available through an AWS Deep Learning Container. With SGLang-Neuron, you can serve models and generate reinforcement learning rollouts with SGLang on AWS Trainium using the same SGLang interface you already know, all running on native PyTorch.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Deploy frontier AI models on AWS Trainium with SGLang-Neuron

Today, Amazon announced that SGLang-Neuron is publicly available and can be accessed through an AWS Deep Learning Container, released by RadixArk in collaboration with Annapurna Labs. With SGLang-Neuron, you can serve models and generate reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts with SGLang on AWS Trainium using the same SGLang interface you use today. Trainium is a portfolio of AWS AI chips that delivers strong economics for AI training and inference at scale. Now, running SGLang on Trainium follows the SGLang workflow you already know: you launch models through SGLang’s server interface and invoke the endpoint using the same generation APIs. Underneath that interface, SGLang-Neuron runs on native PyTorch. With its out-of-tree plugin design, Trainium support and SGLang core develop independently and iterate faster.

How SGLang runs on Trainium

SGLang-Neuron is an out-of-tree plugin that connects SGLang with AWS Trainium. Installing the plugin registers the neuron platform through SGLang’s plugin entry points, and setting 

SGLANG_PLATFORM=neuron
selects it when the server starts. SGLang core continues to provide the API server, request lifecycle, RadixAttention, and prefix-cache bookkeeping. The plugin implements the Trainium-specific models, attention, mixture of experts (MoE), and the graph runner.

TorchNeuron registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device. SGLang-Neuron uses standard PyTorch operations for the model execution path and incorporates kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) for performance. It compiles these operations and kernels into executable programs using 

torch.compile
, which the graph runner prepares and executes during serving.

SGLang-Neuron also supports PD disaggregation. In this configuration, a prefill server computes the prompt KV cache and transfers it to a decode server using NIXL over Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). The decode server then generates the remaining tokens. Each server still uses SGLang’s scheduler and request lifecycle, while the plugin manages the Trainium execution and KV-cache transfer path.

Serving models on AWS Trainium using SGLang-Neuron

To follow this walkthrough, you use a Trainium3 Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance with a 

pytorch-inference-sglang-neuronx
container. Here are the steps:
  • Start the container.
  • Launch the SGLang model server inside the container.
  • Send a request to the model server.

For additional information, please see the SGLang-Neuron getting started guide for setup instructions, and explore the repository documentation for supported models, features, and validated configurations.

Conclusion

SGLang-Neuron brings SGLang’s familiar serving workflow to AWS Trainium through native PyTorch. You can get started by launching the SGLang-Neuron container and following the quickstart to serve a supported model. Try it with your workloads, contribute through the project repository, and share feedback to help shape future model and feature support.

entries.title: How Natera designed an agentic AI system for lab ops with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
entries.summary: Natera built SWARM, an agentic AI system on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that captures institutional lab-operations knowledge and deploys it at scale. This post walks through the full architecture, from knowledge base construction to deployment and evaluation, delivering about 130x faster first response and 96.2% automated coverage across support tickets.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How Natera designed an agentic AI system for lab ops with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

At Natera, a leader in cell-free DNA (cfDNA) testing, keeping lab instruments up and running is critical, because equipment downtime disrupts sample processing. Natera’s lab engineering team, led by Ariel Jirau worked with AWS to build SWARM (Systematic Workflow Analytics and Resolutions Manager), an agentic AI system for lab operations.

This post walks through how the Natera team built an agentic AI system for lab operations using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that captures and deploys institutional knowledge at scale. It describes the full architecture, from knowledge base construction to automated system deployment and evaluation, so you can apply the same patterns to your own operational workflows.

SWARM delivers about 130x faster first response time and 96.2 percent automated coverage across support tickets, giving engineers immediate access to institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives.

The challenge: Knowledge continuity

Natera’s lab operations rely on a wide range of precision instruments spanning multiple equipment families, each with its own failure modes, vendor documentation, and resolution patterns. The service engineering team responsible for maintaining this infrastructure is organized around deep individual expertise rather than standardized playbooks. When a senior technician who had spent years diagnosing a particular instrument family departed, the institutional knowledge they carried was effectively lost. No system existed to capture, organize, or deploy that expertise at scale.

With over 65 tickets per day across three Jira queues and an average first response time of 17.4 hours, instrument downtime delayed lab samples and patient reporting. Hiring more engineers couldn’t keep pace. SWARM had to respond in minutes, deliver accurate diagnostics across a wide range of equipment types, and improve continuously through a structured evaluation loop.

Why Natera chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

The Natera team chose to build SWARM on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a fully managed, extensible service by AWS designed to build, deploy, connect, secure, and operate AI agents at scale. Three core requirements drove the decision:

  • Autonomous processing of high-volume support tickets without human intervention.
  • Deep integration with existing operational tools such as Jira and Confluence.
  • Built-in security and observability (encryption, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) integration, and distributed tracing) without requiring the team to build and maintain custom infrastructure.

“We needed a managed runtime that would let us focus engineering effort on diagnostic accuracy rather than infrastructure plumbing—AgentCore gave us that, along with built-in identity management and the flexibility to swap models without rewriting agent logic,” Jirau said.

AgentCore provides native integration with services including Amazon DynamoDB, a fully managed NoSQL database service, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), and AWS X-Ray, a capability of Amazon CloudWatch.

How SWARM works: Two agents, one skill library

SWARM uses two complementary runtimes sharing a single skill library. The swarm-agent autonomously generates structured diagnostic reports before an engineer opens a ticket, while engineers use swarm-hive to interact in real time, upload images, and explore alternative troubleshooting paths.

“The system does not replace engineers—it gives them access to the full depth of institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives,” Jirau said.

Four layers connect the architecture:

  • The event layer routes Jira tickets through Amazon EventBridge and Amazon SQS.
  • The agent layer hosts swarm-agent, swarm-hive, and the skill library, and delivers diagnostic reports back to engineers.
  • The context layer draws on vendor manuals, historical tickets, and operational data.
  • The observability and delivery layer captures traces, logs, and metrics.

Security architecture

The Natera team’s first architectural decision was where to run the agents. The team required a managed runtime that would handle container orchestration, scaling, and security without requiring them to maintain custom infrastructure. They chose AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, because it hosts both swarm-agent and swarm-hive in a secure, managed environment with built-in identity management and monitoring, avoiding the need to build and operate a custom agent execution layer. You can adopt this pattern regardless of the framework you choose.

The team chose a keyless deployment model because SWARM runs in a clinical environment where credentials exposure is unacceptable. OpenID Connect (OIDC) and AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) generate temporary credentials scoped per deployment, with no long-lived keys in the pipeline. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) enforces least privilege at the component level. Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) with private subnets and VPC endpoints keeps traffic off the public internet. AWS Secrets Manager rotates the few credentials that exist on an automatic 30-day cycle.

GitLab CI runners authenticate to AWS by presenting an OIDC token to an IAM identity provider configured in the account. AWS STS exchanges the token for short-lived credentials scoped to the deployment role (no long-lived access keys are stored in the pipeline). For setup details, see the IAM OIDC provider documentation.

The following example illustrates the pattern: an IAM OIDC trust policy for GitLab CI follows this structure:

These infrastructure-level security controls work in concert with SWARM’s data governance policies. Together they form the full compliance posture required for operating an AI system in a regulated clinical environment.

Compliance and data governance

SWARM runs on HIPAA-eligible AWS services under a Business Associate Agreement (BAA), reflecting Natera’s obligations as a clinical laboratory operator. Every agent invocation is audit-logged (a searchable record that satisfies data access traceability requirements). No patient-identifiable information touches the vector index or the language model. Tickets contain only equipment and workflow metadata. Teams building under HIPAA or similar regulatory frameworks should confirm BAA coverage and data separation requirements before designing the knowledge base pipeline.

Knowledge base and document pipeline construction

Early prototypes using general-purpose retrieval without equipment-specific metadata produced inconsistent results, so the Natera team built a custom document processing pipeline tailored to technical equipment documentation. Amazon Titan Text Embeddings generates vector representations for semantic search, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), converting documents into embeddings stored in batches of 100, a size chosen to balance indexing throughput against API rate limits. For heavily structured source documents with tables and diagrams, investing in a custom parsing pipeline rather than relying on default chunking compounds accuracy gains across every diagnosis.

Amazon Bedrock services, including Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore are available in multiple AWS Regions. For the latest information, see Amazon Bedrock supported Regions and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supported Regions.

The Natera team uses the tiktoken tokenizer with the cl100k_base encoding to measure chunk boundaries. The following example illustrates the pattern, the chunking configuration follows a standard structure:

For more on batch ingestion patterns, see the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases documentation.

“Diagnostic accuracy is a data quality problem first,” Jirau said. “Adding missing vendor manuals for the lowest-scoring instrument family lifted accuracy from 71% to 75% with no model changes.”

This shaped the Natera team’s improvement approach: when accuracy plateaus, the team checks data coverage before model tuning, because gaps in vendor documentation are the most common cause of missed diagnoses. The pipeline reprocesses new or updated documents and refreshes the vector index without disrupting active operations.

Skill library architecture

The Natera team faced a key architectural choice: embed logic directly in agent prompts, or build a separate, versioned skill library. Natera chose the library approach because it makes SWARM auditable and improvable.

“When a diagnosis is wrong, we need to point to a specific skill rather than debug the whole system — that’s why we built a versioned skill library from the start,” Jirau said.

The library contains 33 skills: 24 instrument-specific skills covering the full range of equipment families Natera supports, plus 9 cross-cutting workflow skills that apply broadly across ticket types. Each skill has a defined interface, is independently testable, and is evaluated against the same standards as the overall system, treated as production software, not embedded prompt logic.

The skill architecture follows a clear split: Python handles deterministic tasks such as parsing Jira fields or formatting HTML reports, while large language model (LLM) skills handle language reasoning such as interpreting symptoms, matching vendor documentation, and generating diagnostic narratives. For teams building a multi-skill agent, this split between deterministic Python skills and LLM-powered reasoning skills is one of the highest-impact decisions to make.

Agent runtime deployment

Natera split diagnostic work into two distinct runtimes because autonomous background analysis and interactive engineering collaboration have fundamentally different latency and context requirements. The swarm-agent is built for throughput. It selects skills based on equipment type and symptoms, queries the knowledge base, and produces a structured HTML report with a lead cause hypothesis, ranked troubleshooting steps, and a confidence label. The report is delivered to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and linked to the Jira ticket within minutes. Swarm-hive is designed for depth: engineers can engage in interactive follow-up, upload images, and explore alternative paths, with AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, retaining per-engineer conversational context across sessions.

Because swarm-hive accepts free-form engineer input, prompts are routed through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content filtering.

Event-driven Jira integration

SWARM integrates with Jira through Amazon EventBridge Scheduler and a polling AWS Lambda function, a serverless compute service that runs code in response to events, avoiding webhook configuration. Verified tickets enter an Amazon SQS queue for reliable delivery. DynamoDB handles deduplication using the ticket ID as a partition key with time-to-live (TTL) based expiry, and stores per-run metadata such as status, cost, and token usage to feed the evaluation loop. This 

EventBridge-to-SQS
pattern decouples the agent runtime from the ticketing system’s availability.

The following example illustrates the pattern. The deduplication table uses a minimal schema with TTL-based expiry:

Observability design

Agentic systems with many interacting components are difficult to debug without per-invocation traces, so the Natera team built observability into SWARM before the first production deployment. If you’re running agents in production, per-invocation tracing is non-negotiable: without it, debugging a bad diagnosis means guessing which skill misbehaved.

In a clinical lab environment, where instrument downtime directly impacts patient reporting, the ability to trace, alert on, and audit every agent action isn’t a “nice to have”. It’s a regulatory and operational requirement.

SWARM’s observability stack uses Amazon CloudWatch to capture searchable logs for every run, providing a clear record of operational health. AWS X-Ray traces each run from ticket intake to diagnostic report, recording time and cost per tool call so the team can pinpoint the specific skill responsible when something is slow or expensive rather than guessing. Amazon Simple Notification Service delivers failure alerts by email, while a Slack tracker gives the entire team real-time visibility into agent activity.

Continuous evaluation methodology

SWARM uses a continuous evaluation loop rather than testing once at deployment, which is especially critical for systems handling changing documentation or evolving workflows. On every ticket processed, the agent provides a lead cause hypothesis, ranked troubleshooting steps, and a self-rated confidence label. Engineers record what they found and fixed, and an evaluator grades each response as Accurate, Partial, or Wrong, broken down by instrument family. Results are reviewed to identify where the agent is underperforming, the fix is applied (typically by updating the knowledge base), and the evaluation set is re-run to confirm improvement.

SWARM’s self-rated confidence labels show a directional relationship with actual accuracy. Tickets labeled High confidence achieve 74 percent accuracy across 154 evaluated cases, while Moderate and Low confidence tickets both achieve 65 percent across 78 and 37 cases respectively. Note that Moderate and Low currently share the same accuracy rate. The Low confidence sample size of 37 cases is too small to draw statistically meaningful conclusions, and the Natera team expects the two tiers to diverge as the evaluation dataset expands.

The separation between High and the remaining tiers gives engineers a useful signal for how much weight to place on each diagnosis at the point of reading a diagnostic report.

SWARM performance

The Natera team evaluated SWARM across 524 support tickets to establish a performance baseline. Of the 524 tickets in the evaluation set, 269 received a High, Moderate, or Low confidence label and had a corresponding engineer-verified resolution available for comparison. The remaining tickets were either labeled none or lacked a verified resolution at the time of analysis.

Average first response time dropped from 17.4 hours to roughly 8 minutes (about 130x faster). These measurements were collected from Jira ticket metadata over a 90-day production evaluation period. Coverage matters just as much: 96.2 percent of tickets get an automated first response without an engineer having to initiate the diagnostic process. Coverage was measured as the percentage of incoming tickets that received a SWARM-generated diagnostic report before engineer review.

Lessons from building agentic AI in production

Several architectural decisions in SWARM translate directly to teams building similar systems.

  • Treat chunk size and overlap as tunable parameters. The right values depend on how your source documents are structured.
  • Build traceability into your skill library from the start. When a diagnosis is wrong, you want to point to a specific skill, not debug the whole system.
  • If your workload mixes batch processing with interactive querying, separate them into distinct runtimes.

Getting started

Try these patterns yourself with the AgentCore samples repository, Building Agentic systems on AWS or the Getting Started with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore guide for deploying agents securely at scale. Healthcare and life sciences organizations facing similar challenges with institutional knowledge loss, high-volume operational workflows, or clinical compliance requirements will find that the architectural patterns Natera developed with SWARM provide a replicable, production-tested foundation for building agentic AI systems on AWS.

entries.title: Four Amazon Bedrock inference choices that affect cost
entries.summary: Your Amazon Bedrock inference bill can keep climbing even after you tune prompts and application logic. Four request-level choices (cache duration, service tier, reasoning effort, and maxTokens) change how many tokens the service processes and the rate applied. We show how we tested each and how to verify the effect.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Four Amazon Bedrock inference choices that affect cost

Your Amazon Bedrock inference bill can keep climbing after you tune prompts and application logic. Request-level choices can still change how many tokens the service processes and the rate applied to them. Cache duration, service tier, reasoning effort, and 

maxTokens
can affect cost without changing your model or prompt.

Each choice depends on the model and workload. This post shows how we tested each choice and how to verify its effect from response metadata, logs, and billing data.

To try these settings yourself, start with the Amazon Bedrock Samples notebooks Mixed TTL Caching and Tenant Isolation with Prompt Caching. For 

maxTokens
and reasoning effort, see the 01-low-effort folder of the sample-code-for-genai-cost-management-workshop GitHub repo. Each sample sets its own model ID, so change it, and the inference parameters, to match the model you call. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Models at a glance. For broader decisions such as model selection, batch inference, routing, and distillation, see Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock.

Where inference cost comes from

Every Amazon Bedrock response carries usage metadata. Input and output tokens bill at the rate for the model and tier that served the request. Cache reads and writes use separate token counters, and reasoning tokens count as output tokens.

Prompt cache duration

Repeated system instructions, tool definitions, or reference context can be processed again when the cache expires before the next request. The Prompt caching for faster model inference guide lists 5-minute and 1-hour time-to-live (TTL) values for supported Anthropic models. It also lists a 30-minute minimum TTL for supported GPT-5.6 models. Support and API fields depend on the model, so check the current support matrix before selecting a duration.

For supported models, Amazon Bedrock also offers implicit prompt caching, which attempts to reuse eligible prompt prefixes without cache controls in your request. Because implicit caching is best effort and doesn’t guarantee a cache hit, the duration choices in this section apply to explicit caching.

This Converse API signature requests a 1-hour entry on models that support it:

For supported Anthropic models, InvokeModel places the same 

ttl
value in 
cache_control
.

A longer duration is not automatically cheaper. The Amazon Bedrock Pricing page lists separate rates for 5-minute writes, 1-hour writes, and cache reads. For Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 and Anthropic Claude Opus 5 on Amazon Bedrock, a 5-minute write costs 1.25 times the input rate. A 1-hour write costs 2 times, and a cache read costs 0.1 times.

These rates set the break-even, assuming each request reuses the exact prefix and each cache read refreshes the TTL. A 5-minute cache pays back on the first reuse within 5 minutes. When requests for the same prefix arrive more than 5 minutes apart, it rewrites at 1.25 times on every request. The 1-hour cache is then cheaper from the second request within the hour.

Cache rates and checkpoint minimums differ by model. Check the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page and the prompt caching guide for the model you call. Rerun the comparison for your model, then confirm it with cache read and write tokens after rollout.

Keep stable content before dynamic content, meet the model’s checkpoint minimum, and use on-demand inference because prompt caching doesn’t work with batch inference.

Changing a cached prefix, including a system instruction or tool definition, causes a miss and a new write. Checkpoints are evaluated in the order tools, system, then messages, so a change in an earlier section also invalidates the later ones. Version prompts that change often so each version gets its own cache entry. We ran six calls on Claude Sonnet 5 with a 1-hour checkpoint, changing the system prompt once and the tool definition once. Each change produced zero cache reads and a new write.

AWS describes cache entries as scoped to your account and Region, not to your tenants. In a multi-tenant application, prepend a tenant-specific SHA-256 hash to the cacheable prefix. The Optimizing cost and latency with Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for Anthropic models post describes this pattern. Enforce tenant authorization before you build the prompt. The hash partitions entries inside one account. If a regulated workload needs a hard data boundary, keep each tenant in a separate AWS account.

Keep the 5-minute default for frequent reuse. Move from it to a longer supported duration when the same prefix recurs at least twice an hour with gaps longer than 5 minutes. To beat no caching at all, the 1-hour cache needs three requests an hour.

Service tiers for latency-tolerant workloads

Background jobs, evaluation harnesses, nightly summarization, and backfills don’t always need the latency profile used by interactive requests. For models that support Flex, select it with this request signature:

Use 

default
, not 
standard
, to request the Standard tier. You can also omit 
serviceTier
:

Tier support is model-specific, so record support by exact model version. The Amazon Nova 2 Lite and OpenAI gpt-oss-120b model cards list Flex as supported. The cards for Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 and Anthropic Claude Opus 5 on Amazon Bedrock list it as not supported. A Flex request to an unsupported model fails with a 

ValidationException
instead of silently running on Standard. Our request to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 returned that error.

If your policy allows Standard as a fallback, catch the unsupported-tier error and retry once with 

default
. Don’t retry every 
ValidationException
, because malformed requests raise it too. Cap application-level retries. The bounded retry strategy of the AWS SDK handles throttling and transient errors.

Set your own deadline for Flex requests. A supported response reports the resolved tier, which you can also verify with Amazon CloudWatch 

ResolvedServiceTier
. See Service tiers for optimizing performance and cost and the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page for the exact model you call.

We tested Flex on Amazon Nova 2 Lite with 200 

default
requests and 200 
flex
requests, sent in interleaved pairs. Both tiers processed the same number of input and output tokens. All 400 requests resolved to the requested tier, and the median latency difference was too small to separate from noise. At the time of writing, the published Flex rate for Nova 2 Lite in us-west-2 is half the Standard rate, and our bill reflected that. Check the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page for current rates. Keep latency-sensitive traffic on 
default
.

Adaptive thinking effort

Reasoning tokens bill as output tokens. Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 use adaptive thinking at 

high
effort by default, even when a request omits the 
thinking
field. An application moved from Claude Sonnet 4.6 without changes starts billing thinking tokens, and 
maxTokens
now caps thinking plus response text. Claude Haiku 5.5 defaults to 
medium
. All three models support 
low
, 
medium
, 
high
, 
xhigh
, and 
max
. Lower the effort for a task with this request signature:

Keep effort in 

output_config
, not inside 
thinking
. Check Adaptive thinking whenever you change models.

We tested a tool-calling agent on Claude Opus 5. Its three tasks follow the design in Build long-horizon agents with Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock, and each has one correct answer. We ran each task eight times at every effort level. The table shows median output tokens:

EffortCorrect runsMedian output tokensChange from low (95% interval)
low24 of 24936baseline
medium24 of 241,484+59% (50% to 78%)
high (default)24 of 242,521+169% (112% to 190%)
xhigh24 of 242,964+217% (170% to 260%)
max24 of 243,762+302% (180% to 402%)

Accuracy at lower effort depends on the model and the task. Measure on tasks shaped like yours.

On the Amazon Bedrock Samples Invoke Bedrock model for code generation workload, median output tokens were 676 at 

low
and 743 at 
high
, a difference within run-to-run variation. The programs we graded passed at each effort level.

Use per-request output-token counts, CloudWatch 

AWS/Bedrock OutputTokenCount
, invocation logs, and a task pass rate to evaluate the choice. Start below 
high
for routine, well-bounded tasks. Keep 
high
where your quality tests show that the task needs it. A token reduction that breaks the task is not a saving.

Output token limits

maxTokens
is an application output ceiling. It limits the output that a bad prompt, regression, or loop can produce before the request stops. The quota rule is documented in How tokens are counted in Amazon Bedrock. Amazon Bedrock deducts your input tokens plus 
maxTokens
when a request starts, so an oversized value reduces concurrency.

An output ceiling isn’t a safety control. Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails as a standard responsible AI control in production generative AI workloads. Guardrails can filter content, detect prompt attacks, and check grounding on supported inputs and responses. See Detect and filter harmful content by using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

Set 

maxTokens
per task type after observing a representative output-token distribution:

See Inference using Converse API for the request parameters.

In our test on Claude Sonnet 5, five normal outputs peaked at 103 tokens, so we set an illustrative fence of 155 tokens with headroom. We then sent the same deliberately verbose prompt with adaptive thinking disabled, once under a 2,048-token ceiling and once under the 155-token fence. The first request generated 2,048 output tokens and the second generated 155, so the fence avoided 1,893 output tokens. Both stopped at 

max_tokens
, so both responses were truncated. The fence limits spend but does not make an unsuitable prompt useful, and in a multi-turn or agentic chain a truncated turn can break the steps after it.

For production calibration, compare the 95th and 99th percentiles (P95 and P99) for each task type and add headroom to the selected percentile. With adaptive thinking on, 

maxTokens
also caps thinking tokens, so calibrate with thinking enabled. P95 limits exposure more aggressively but accepts more truncation risk. P99 preserves more valid long-tail responses at a higher ceiling. Monitor 
max_tokens
stops and investigate the request before raising the task’s limit.

Putting it together

Use the same test loop for each setting: confirm model support, change one request choice, measure tokens or cost, and track quality or completion. If you route across models, keep a capability record for each model version, Region, and API: supported cache duration, service tiers, reasoning levels, and output ceiling. Validate each request against that record before you send it, then check the response for the resolved tier and cache counters.

Conclusion

All four choices live in the inference request. Recheck support when you change models, then change one setting at a time and measure the result in your application.

Use these resources to evaluate the choices for your workload:

  • Amazon Bedrock console: console.aws.amazon.com/bedrock.
  • Prompt caching: Prompt caching for faster model inference.
  • Service tiers: Service tiers for optimizing performance and cost.
  • Adaptive thinking: Adaptive thinking.
  • Responsible AI controls: Detect and filter harmful content by using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.
  • Related reading: Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock.

entries.title: Tokenomics at scale: Track and cap Amazon Bedrock spend per IAM principal with CUR 2.0 and AWS Budgets
entries.summary: Get per-identity Amazon Bedrock cost visibility and enforceable spend limits using only AWS-native features, with no application code for the common case. Attribute spend with IAM principal tags, report with CUR 2.0 or Cost Explorer, and enforce with AWS Budgets actions that apply a Deny policy when a threshold is crossed.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Tokenomics at scale: Track and cap Amazon Bedrock spend per IAM principal with CUR 2.0 and AWS Budgets

Generative AI spend is hard to attribute. Before an organization expands AI access, CFOs and CTOs usually want three answers: what do we spend per person or per team, can we cap it, and how much work does it take to get there.

In our previous post, Tokenomics at Scale: How Jamf Built Real-Time Spend Enforcement for Amazon Bedrock, we explained a custom enforcement loop built on AWS IAM Identity Center, Amazon Athena over Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs, and AWS Lambda. This approach gives near-real-time control, but it requires code you then own and operate.

This post shows how to get per-identity Amazon Bedrock cost visibility and enforceable spend limits using only AWS-native features, with no application code to write for the common case. The approach relies on three things: IAM principal attribution, which Amazon Bedrock records automatically; AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) 2.0 or AWS Cost Explorer for reporting; and AWS Budgets with budget actions for enforcement. By the end, you will have per-identity cost reporting and an automatic guardrail that restricts Amazon Bedrock access when a threshold is crossed.

Solution overview

The solution has three parts: attribute, report, and enforce.

Attribute. Amazon Bedrock captures the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal identity, the IAM user or role, for every inference request. This happens automatically, with no change to your Amazon Bedrock model inference calls. If several people share one role, you add per-user detail with session tags passed at role assumption time. If each person or application has its own role, principal tags on the role are enough.

Report. Activate those tags as cost allocation tags, then read the data either in Cost Explorer for a console-only view, or in a CUR 2.0 data export for detailed line-item analysis and SQL queries.

Enforce. Create an AWS Budget scoped to Amazon Bedrock and filtered to one identity or tag value, then attach a budget action that applies a Deny IAM policy when the threshold is crossed.

The following sections show each part in more detail, alongside the implementation steps.

Prerequisites

To deploy this solution, you need:

  • An AWS account with Amazon Bedrock model access enabled.
  • Permissions to tag IAM principal, activate cost allocation tags, create data exports, and create budgets and budget actions.
  • Amazon Bedrock accessed through IAM roles or IAM users.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with appropriate credentials.
  • A CUR 2.0 data export and an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket to receive it. (optional, for detailed line-item analysis).
  • Amazon Athena. (optional, for querying the export).

AWS Billing Console access is managed separately from most IAM permissions. Confirm you have it before starting.

Walkthrough

Before configuring anything, check what you already have. Amazon Bedrock records caller identity for every inference request automatically. Open Cost Explorer, filter Service to Amazon Bedrock, and group by the available identity or tag dimension. For accounts where each application or person already uses a distinct IAM role, this may be all the visibility you need.

To configure additional visibility:

  • Step 1 gives you identity-level visibility.
  • Steps 2 through 4 add tag dimensions and detailed reporting.
  • Step 5 adds enforcement.

Step 1: Decide how identity maps to your users

How you tag depends on how your IAM principals are organized.

One role per person or per application. Attach principal tags directly to each IAM role or user. These are static and apply to every request from that principal. Use the IAM console, or the AWS CLI:

A shared role used by several people, or a gateway. Principal tags cannot distinguish users on a shared role, because every session carries the same tags. Use session tags instead, passed when the role is assumed. Session tags are dynamic and can vary per session. If a session tag and a principal tag share a key, the session tag wins for that session.

The role’s trust policy must allow 

sts:TagSession
. Session tags can be passed three ways:
  • sts:AssumeRole
    with 
    --tags
    , for a gateway assuming a role per user or tenant.
  • AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
    , with tags in the https://aws.amazon.com/tags claim of the OpenID Connect (OIDC) ID token (this is a claim name, not a URL you browse to).
  • AssumeRoleWithSAML
    , by mapping 
    PrincipalTag:*
    attributes in the identity provider’s Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertion.

If your organization already captures a claim like 

saml:sub
for other purposes, that alone does not make it available here. Your identity provider must separately map that attribute to a 
PrincipalTag:*
SAML attribute statement, and the role’s trust policy must allow 
sts:TagSession
, before it flows through as a session tag. The two integrations draw from the same SAML assertion but are configured independently. Common tag keys are user, team, Department, CostCenter, and Environment. You can apply up to 50 principal or session tags per IAM user or role.

Step 2: Activate cost allocation tags

Tags do not appear in billing data until you activate them.

  • Open the AWS Billing and Cost Management Console.
  • Choose Cost allocation tags.
  • Filter by type IAM principal.
  • Select your tag keys and choose Activate.

In an AWS Organization, activate IAM principal cost allocation tags in the management account (payer). Member accounts cannot activate them independently.

Two things to expect:

  • A tag key only appears in this list after the principal has made at least one Amazon Bedrock call, so make a test call first if the list looks empty.
  • It might take up to 24 hours for a newly applied tag key to appear for activation, then up to another 24 hours after you activate it before it begins populating billing data.

Activation does not apply retroactively by default, so activate tags before you need the data.

Step 3: Create a CUR 2.0 data export that includes caller identity

Skip this step if Cost Explorer is enough for your reporting.

  • In the Billing and Cost Management console, choose Data Exports.
  • Choose Create and create a CUR 2.0 (Standard) export.
  • Under Additional export content, select Include caller identity (IAM principal) allocation data.
  • Under Time granularity, select Hourly.
  • Under Report data integration, select Amazon Athena. This sets the file format to Parquet and, importantly, delivers a setup script to your S3 bucket alongside the export data.
  • Choose the destination Amazon S3 bucket.
  • Run the delivered setup script (or the Glue crawler/DDL it defines) once. This is what actually creates the Glue Data Catalog table you’ll query in Step 4. The preceding console flow does not create it for you automatically.

If you already have a CUR 2.0 export created before enabling identity attribution, it will not include identity data retroactively. Create a new export with the caller identity option selected. In the export, principal and session tags appear as columns prefixed 

iamPrincipal/
, and resource tags as 
resourceTags/
. For example, a tag key team appears as 
iamPrincipal/team
. AWS publishes a ready-made query set for this exact pattern in aws-samples/sample-cur-iam-principal-bedrock-tracking.

Step 4: Read the data

The following diagram compares the two ways to read the data: a console-only path through Cost Explorer, and a SQL path over the CUR 2.0 export with Amazon Athena.

Console path, no custom code. Cost Explorer, filtered to Amazon Bedrock and grouped by your tag key, gives per-team or per-user spend as a chart and table. This covers most recurring reporting needs and requires no query authoring.

SQL path, low code. Point Amazon Athena at the CUR 2.0 export to group spend by 

iamPrincipal/team
and usage type:

Things to note:

  • Service code: Amazon Bedrock spend can be recorded under more than one 
    product_servicecode
    value, for example, 
    AmazonBedrock
    and 
    AmazonBedrockService
    .
  • Table name: The table name (
    cur2_view
    ) is whatever the setup script from Step 3 named it when it created the Glue table. Check the script or your Glue catalog if it differs. Column names match the CUR 2.0 Parquet schema regardless of table name.
  • Billing-period column. Confirm how your export exposes the period. Some exports use 
    billing_period
    (YYYY-MM). Others partition on a start-date or year/month column.

Two notes worth carrying into any query you write.

  • Count all token types: Amazon Bedrock bills four token types, each at a different rate: input, output, cache read, and cache write. Each is a separate line item with its own usage type and unit price, so summing only input and output undercounts. The gap is largest for workloads that use prompt caching heavily. Refer to the AWS document Understanding Amazon Bedrock pricing in CUR for the latest information.
  • Match the rate to the line item, not the model: Amazon Bedrock pricing in CUR is determined by three things: the token type, the service tier, and whether the request was routed through cross-Region inference. In-Region and cross-Region requests are priced differently, and service tier is reflected in the usage type as well. The usage type carries a suffix indicating cross-Region routing and service tier, so if your workloads mix these, match the rate to each line item rather than applying one rate per model. Refer to the CUR usage type examples for examples.

Step 5: Add enforcement with AWS Budgets and budget actions

AWS Budgets performs the attach, so there is no custom code for this workflow. Budget actions attach to a specific IAM user, group, or role. This isolates one person’s access only if that person already has their own role. If your Amazon Bedrock traffic runs through a role that many people share, a Deny action attached to that role blocks everyone on it, not only the person who crossed the threshold. The following diagram explains the enforcement workflow.

AWS Budgets can run an action when a threshold is crossed. Available actions include applying a custom IAM policy, applying a service control policy (SCP), and targeting Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) or Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) instances. For this use case, the IAM policy action is the relevant one.

First, create the Deny policy the action will attach. This example denies the higher-cost models while leaving a lower-cost model available, so the user can keep working:

Replace 

[HIGHER-COST-MODEL-ID]
with the model ID you want to deny in your environment.

Then set up permissions and the budget itself.

There are two distinct roles here, and the AWS managed policy only covers one of them:

Your own user or role (the one configuring the budget) needs the AWS managed policy 

AWSBudgetsActionsWithAWSResourceControlAccess
. It grants budgets permissions plus the conditioned 
iam:PassRole
needed to hand your budget action role to AWS Budgets.

The IAM role AWS Budgets assumes to perform the action is not covered by a single named managed policy for this use case. Create it with a trust policy that allows the principal 

budgets.amazonaws.com
to assume it (scoped with 
aws:SourceArn
and 
aws:SourceAccount
conditions), and a permissions policy granting 
iam:AttachRolePolicy
and 
iam:DetachRolePolicy
(and 
organizations:AttachPolicy
and 
organizations:DetachPolicy
if you are also using SCPs). Refer to Setting up a role for AWS Budgets to run budget actions for the grantable permissions.
  • Create the budget action role described earlier.
  • Create a cost budget scoped to Amazon Bedrock, filtered to the identity or tag value you want to cap.
  • In Configure alerts, add an alert threshold. Choose Actual for realized spend or Forecasted to act before the spend lands.
  • Under Attach actions, choose Add Action, select the budget actions role, and choose the IAM policy action. Select the Deny policy and the IAM user, group, or role to attach it to.
  • For automatic enforcement, choose Yes to run the action automatically. Choose No to require a human to approve each action from the Alert details page.
  • Configure at least one notification so the affected user is told why access changed.

You can attach multiple actions to a single threshold, and multiple thresholds to one budget. That is how you build tiers: for example, deny the premium model at 80 percent and the mid-tier model at 100 percent, while never denying the low-cost model.

Only the management account can apply SCPs, and from the management account you can apply an SCP to another account.

Considerations

AWS Budgets is not near-real-time: Budget data refreshes up to three times a day, so spend can overshoot a threshold before the action runs.

Cost allocation tags are not retroactive: Expect up to 24 hours for a newly applied tag key to appear, then up to another 24 hours after you activate it before it begins populating billing data.

CUR does not contain per-request line items: Both classic CUR and CUR 2.0 aggregate Amazon Bedrock cost by usage type, operation, and pricing/resource attributes over an hour or a day.

IAM principal fields require CUR 2.0: The legacy CUR format does not include them. Per-token cost breakdowns are available in both formats.

Session tags are bound at AssumeRole time, not per request. Their values are constant for every call made with that session’s credentials, and they surface only as aggregated billing data. Session tags are not written to model invocation logs. Logs capture the caller’s 

identity.arn
. To distinguish users on a shared session at the request level, use a per-user 
RoleSessionName
, or set the user in request metadata on each call.

Budget actions attach to IAM users, groups, and roles. If your users are federated and have no standing IAM identity, the action needs a role to target. This is why the pattern works best when each person or application has its own role. If your users share a role or are federated without their own role, see our previous post for a per-user enforcement approach.

A shared gateway role collapses attribution by default. With a large language model (LLM) gateway, the identity captured is the gateway’s execution role.

New models need attention. Usage types are model-specific. When you enable a new model, confirm it appears in your queries and budget filters as expected rather than assuming it is covered.

Decision framework

RequirementRecommended path
Quick reportingCost Explorer grouped by identity
Per-team reportingCost Explorer with activated tags (Steps 1, 2, and 4)
Detailed line-item analysisCUR 2.0 export (Steps 1 through 4)
EnforcementAWS Budgets with budget actions (Steps 1 and 5)

Cleanup

To avoid ongoing charges, delete all the resources you created.

Conclusion

In this post, you learned how to get per-identity Amazon Bedrock cost visibility and enforceable spend limits using only AWS-native features, with no application code to write for the common case. As generative AI adoption scales, the organizations that win will be the ones that can answer the tokenomics question with confidence: what do we spend per person or per team, can we cap it, and how much work does it take to get there.

Now, it’s your turn to start exploring. We are here to help, and if you need further assistance, reach out to AWS Support and your AWS account team.

entries.title: Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock
entries.summary: Comparing per-token prices hides the real cost of running a model on Amazon Bedrock. This post shows how to calculate the true cost per task across four hidden cost drivers, reduce it with caching, routing, and output constraints, and prove agent ROI with human baselines, holdout experiments, and a five-dimension scorecard.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock

Part 1 of this series built the operating model that controls Amazon Bedrock spend: attribution with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal tags and Cost and Usage Report 2.0, observability with model invocation logging, enforcement at three tiers, and a review cadence. That layer answers who spent it, and you can stop them. It can’t tell you whether the spend was well spent.

This post answers two questions that Part 1 deliberately left open. First: Why is this workflow expensive? The answer requires thinking in cost per task, not cost per token. Second: Is the agent better than the humans were? The answer requires baselines, controlled experiments, and a scorecard tied to decisions.

In this post, you learn a framework for calculating true model cost (including four hidden cost drivers that the pricing page doesn’t show), techniques for reducing cost per task through caching, routing, and output constraints, and a discipline for measuring agent ROI with human baselines, holdout experiments, and a five-dimension scorecard. This post is written for two audiences: the application and platform engineers who own the optimization levers, and the product owners and FinOps partners who need to justify agent spend to leadership.

Cost per task, not cost per token

Price per token invites quick comparison, but it doesn’t reflect what you actually pay. The published rate reflects the cost of a single token. Your bill reflects the cost of completing a task. A task is one complete unit of work your application asks a model to do: resolve one support email, extract fields from one invoice, or answer one user question. A task runs from the request through to a usable result, however many model calls it takes.

The lower-priced model might not be the cheaper one to run. A cheaper model might fragment your text into more tokens, pad responses with filler, misread your tool schema and loop through corrections, or burn thousands of reasoning tokens before answering. None of these costs appear on the Bedrock pricing page.

The four hidden cost drivers

Four model characteristics determine what that published rate actually costs you on your workload.

Tokenizer efficiency

A token isn’t a word, and it is not equal across models. Every model family uses a different tokenizer and vocabulary. The same text, code, or JSON payload splits into different token counts. If Model A’s list price is 15 percent lower but its tokenizer needs 40 percent more tokens for your data (common with structured schemas and numerical arrays), Model B is cheaper. The gap widens for non-English text: many tokenizers fragment non-Latin scripts into two to three times more tokens than the equivalent English.

Output alignment and verbosity

Output tokens commonly cost 3–5x more than input tokens (the ratio varies by family. Refer to the Bedrock pricing page). A model that ignores formatting constraints like “return only raw JSON” makes you pay that output premium for filler words. A model that follows formatting instructions closely saves money by generating fewer of these more expensive output tokens.

Agentic loop efficiency

Agentic workflows change the cost math entirely. Tool use (function calling) lets a model invoke external functions, requiring a multi-turn loop: analyze the prompt, decide to call a tool, wait for the observation, generate an answer. Each turn re-sends the full conversation history and tool results as input tokens. A model that takes four turns (each one re-sending a larger context payload) costs far more than one that finishes in a single pass.

Reasoning overhead

Many models support extended thinking, working through a chain of thought before the visible answer. Reasoning tokens bill as output tokens, so a model that thinks for 2,000 tokens before a 200-token answer bills you for 2,200. Some models redact the reasoning while still charging for it. Start with reasoning turned off and enable it only when benchmarks show a quality gap that justifies the cost.

Cost per task: A worked example

Consider an agentic workflow that reads a 750-word customer email, extracts entities, calls an API to verify account status, and outputs strict JSON. The following comparison uses illustrative prices (always benchmark against your own data and current Bedrock pricing):

MetricModel A (lower list price)Model B (higher list price)
Input list price$0.50 / 1M tokens$1.00 / 1M tokens
Output list price$1.50 / 1M tokens$3.00 / 1M tokens
Tokenizer efficiency (turn 1 input)1,500 tokens1,000 tokens
Output verbosity (final response)450 tokens150 tokens
Agentic loops required3 turns (error correction)1 turn (zero-shot)
Cumulative input tokens, all turns6,1501,000
Cumulative output tokens, all turns750150
Total task cost$0.0042$0.00145

Model A: (6,150 x $0.50 + 750 x $1.50) / 1,000,000 = $0.0042

Model B: (1,000 x $1.00 + 150 x $3.00) / 1,000,000 = $0.00145

Why the 2x-priced model costs 65 percent less: three compounding factors. Model A’s tokenizer fragments the email into 50 percent more tokens, inflating every input payload. It pads its JSON with filler, tripling output tokens. And it misaligns with the tool schema, needing two correction turns that each re-send a growing history.

Cost per successful task

The preceding example assumes both models eventually succeed. In production they won’t, and a failure is rarely free. The formulas:

For retry-until-success workflows:

cost per successful task = cost per attempt / success rate

For escalate-on-failure workflows:

cost per successful task = cost per attempt + (1 - success rate) x escalation cost

Input further splits into three buckets when prompt caching is active: uncached input at base rate, cache reads below base rate, and cache writes above base rate.

Measuring it on your own workload

Which model is actually cheaper only shows up when you benchmark against your own data. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation is the managed feature for the quality half of that: define criteria, upload your prompt datasets, and get scored results with automatic metrics and optional human review, with no custom infrastructure required.

Quality scores alone don’t produce a bill, though. Three more Bedrock features supply the token and turn counts you price against them:

  • CountTokens returns the input token count a given model would charge for a given payload without running inference. It’s the cheapest way to compare tokenizer efficiency (driver #1) across candidates before you spend anything on generation.
  • Model invocation response carries a 
    usage
    block with 
    inputTokens
    , 
    outputTokens
    , 
    cacheReadInputTokens
    , and 
    cacheWriteInputTokens
    . Accumulating those across the turns of a single task gives you the four terms of the preceding cost-per-attempt formula. One gotcha: when caching is enabled, 
    inputTokens
    counts only the uncached tokens, so your total input volume is 
    inputTokens + cacheReadInputTokens + cacheWriteInputTokens
    . Sum them to know the footprint, but price them separately, since the three bill at different rates. Evaluate this multiple times throughout your journey and set the cache checkpoints based on what is the active current load. The drift in cache checkpoints happens as the application progresses and the tools become stale. This means that you will be writing more to the cache in 3 months from now when the drift has happened. Evaluating your data constantly for optimal cache usage becomes a primary lever to reduce cost.
  • Model invocation logging writes per-invocation token counts to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch Logs, so you can measure turns-to-completion against real production traffic instead of a sample. Tag calls with request metadata to slice those logged token counts by team, feature, or experiment. However, these are log fields, not cost allocation tags, and never appear in AWS Cost Explorer or your Cost and Usage Report. Application inference profiles do reach both, at a grain of one usage type per day. That grain is right for chargeback but too coarse for cost per task. Multiplying logged token counts by the published rates gives you a near real-time estimate rather than an invoice. It won’t reflect commitments, batch pricing, or provisioned throughput unless you model them. Reconcile against your Cost and Usage Report before you treat it as the bill.

Reducing cost per task: Four levers

Each of the four drivers has a lever, and each is documented in depth. Prompt caching cuts the re-sent context that made Model A expensive, which makes it the largest win on agentic paths. Intelligent prompt routing sends the easy requests to a cheaper model in the same family. A tool schema plus a maxTokens cap holds verbosity down more reliably than prose instructions do, and extended thinking stays off until a benchmark shows it earns its cost back. Batch inference halves the rate on bulk single-turn work, though it rules out tool calling and multi-turn exchange.

Proving agent ROI: Describe the human baseline

Efficient isn’t the same as valuable. An agent can be perfectly optimized and still not be worth running. The question that decides budgets is: is the agent better than the humans were?

Document the human process first

The biggest mistake in agent ROI is trying to prove value without first describing the human workflow. Before building or scaling an agent, write down the current process in operational terms: what triggers the work, which human roles are involved, where the handoffs sit, how completion is defined. This sounds like bureaucracy. It’s actually measurement design. Every instrumentation decision downstream (what counts as a run, what counts as success, where human time is spent) falls out of this description.

Measure the baseline before the agent ships

With the process described, measure the human baseline over a meaningful window: time to completion, queue time, active effort, reopen rate, escalation rate, cost per task, and outcome quality. Baselines must be measured before the agent goes live, not reconstructed from memory after the fact. Retrospective baselines are systematically flattering to the agent: people remember the average case and forget the fast ones.

Instrument the workflow as an experiment

After the baseline exists, instrument the agent workflow as an experiment from day one. Every run gets a trace ID, and every meaningful step is observable. A workflow-run record aggregates everything above the model call into a single analyzable unit:

Three fields deserve emphasis:

experiment block: Stamped at run creation and propagated into Bedrock request metadata, so model-level and workflow-level records join cleanly.

humanMinutes: What most teams omit and most need. Without it, “the agent did the work” silently excludes the 35 minutes a human spent reviewing it.

revenueEventId: The hook that makes revenue attribution possible later. It costs nothing to record and can’t be reconstructed afterward.

The rule: If the workflow telemetry can’t answer the business question, the instrumentation is incomplete.

Join cost to outcomes

With invocation logs landing in Amazon S3 (Part 1) and workflow-run records in your analytics store, one join produces the metrics that matter. Amazon Bedrock logs record tokens, not dollars, so first build a view that prices each invocation from token counts and your model rate sheet, aggregated by run ID. Then query with Amazon Athena:

Note: Column names and join keys shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema and workflow telemetry store, which might vary by implementation.

Cost per successful outcome, retries per success, and human minutes per success are the three numbers that survive contact with a skeptical CFO. Cost per call flatters agents that loop. Cost per success doesn’t. Note the variant grouping: the same query, split by experiment arm, is the ROI comparison.

Compare agents and humans correctly

The most credible evaluation is an A/B or holdout test. Controlled treatment and control groups compare the agent-assisted workflow against the human baseline without confusing the result with market, seasonal, or organizational changes.

For customer-facing or revenue-linked workflows, randomize at the visitor, lead, account, or case level. For internal workflows (support operations, coding assistants), use matched cohorts: teams, repository groups, or pods.

The comparison covers four dimensions:

Efficiency: time to completion, hours recovered, queue-time reduction.

Quality: error rate, approval rate, reopen rate, escalation rate.

Cost: cost per task, cost per successful outcome, total cost to serve.

Business value: conversion lift, retention lift, expansion rate, revenue per rep or per workflow.

If the agent improves one dimension while meaningfully degrading another, the result is ambiguous and the deployment needs tuning.

Revenue: The hardest metric

Efficiency gains are the easiest part of the ROI story to prove. Revenue impact is harder, and it is the metric leadership funds against. In revenue-adjacent workflows, measure whether the agent improves conversion, time-to-response, deal progression, or revenue per rep. Holdout tests are the most reliable way to separate incremental revenue attributable to the agent from general business momentum.

When revenue lift is real, the conversation changes. The organization stops asking whether the Bedrock bill went up and starts asking whether the additional spend is buying a meaningful increase in business output.

The scorecard

Based on what we have observed working with customers, a strong operating model doesn’t require fifty metrics. What works is a small scorecard tied to decisions, reviewed on a regular cadence for every production agent.

The following thresholds are starting points, not prescriptions. Calibrate them against your own fleet data and organizational context.

DimensionMetricGreenYellowRed
AdoptionActive users / intended users>70%40-70%<40%
QualityTasks completed without rework>90%75-90%<75%
EfficiencyHours recovered per week>target50-100% of target<50% of target
CostCost per successful outcome≤budget1-1.5x budget>1.5x budget
Business impactKPI lift compared to baselineSignificantMarginalNone or negative

Green means scale: the agent beats baseline while meeting cost and quality thresholds. Yellow means tune: promising but needs work. Red means retire or redesign: the agent consumes cost without enough measurable value. The willingness to actually retire a red agent is what makes the rest of the scorecard credible.

Conclusion

In this post, you learned how to calculate the true cost of a model by accounting for four hidden cost drivers (tokenizer efficiency, output alignment, agentic loop efficiency, and reasoning overhead), how to reduce cost per task through prompt caching, model routing, output constraints, and batch inference, and how to prove agent ROI by measuring human baselines, instrumenting workflows as experiments, joining cost to outcomes, and running holdout comparisons.

The cost optimization half answers “why is this expensive and how do I fix it.” The ROI half answers “is the agent better than the humans were.” Together with Part 1’s operating model (attribute, observe, enforce, optimize, operate), they form a complete framework: you can see who spent it, explain why, reduce the waste, and justify what remains.

To get started, benchmark your top model candidates against your own prompts using Amazon Bedrock model evaluation, capture tokens and turns from the 

usage
block or your invocation logs, price them against current Bedrock pricing, and divide by success rate. For ROI measurement, consult the Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens for agent cost governance best practices.

If you have found other techniques for reducing cost per task or measuring agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock, let us know in the comments.

entries.title: Building a self-service LLM gateway with Amazon Bedrock and LiteLLM
entries.summary: Build a self-service LLM gateway with LiteLLM on AWS Fargate that puts Amazon Bedrock foundation models behind an OpenAI-compatible API. Developers get instant access through a single API key, while platform teams gain per-user cost controls, quota isolation, and observability.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Building a self-service LLM gateway with Amazon Bedrock and LiteLLM

Developers want AI coding assistants with minimal setup. With a large language model (LLM) gateway and LiteLLM, they can quickly access foundation models (FMs) available on Amazon Bedrock while you gain visibility and usage control. Platform teams need to monitor latency and errors, finance teams need to attribute inference costs to teams and projects, and security teams need consistent access controls. An LLM gateway can help address these needs by providing a centrally managed access point to the models that power coding assistants.

In this post, we show how to build a self-service LLM gateway using Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles with LiteLLM running on AWS Fargate to abstract Amazon Bedrock behind an OpenAI-compatible API. With this pattern, developers can access foundation models through a single API with a dedicated key while you gain per-user cost controls and model performance observability. By the end, you will understand the pattern well enough to build your own version from the illustrative snippets and AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) constructs. This post uses Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku models for example purposes. For a list of models and availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

This LLM gateway pattern follows a straightforward request flow from the developer, through the LiteLLM layer, to Amazon Bedrock and the underlying FM. The following diagram illustrates the production topology behind that flow. For simplicity, we don’t cover the addition of Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, such as content filtering and grounding, but you would normally include appropriate responsible AI controls before deploying to production.

A developer’s OpenAI-compatible client reaches the LLM gateway through Amazon Route 53, Amazon CloudFront, and an Application Load Balancer (ALB). It authenticates to LiteLLM on Fargate with a per-user API key. Behind that, the request draws on Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) (PostgreSQL) for virtual-key and spend state. It also interacts with Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey as a cache, and AWS Secrets Manager for secrets. LiteLLM then ultimately invokes Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles using a scoped AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) task role. Amazon CloudWatch captures requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM) metrics and the quota alarm.

The architecture consists of these core components:

  • LiteLLM on AWS Fargate: LiteLLM provides a proxy that exposes an OpenAI-compatible API. We run it on an AWS Fargate task with target-tracking Auto Scaling on CPU utilization. Developers point their tools at this endpoint and don’t interact with Amazon Bedrock directly.
  • Self-service portal: LiteLLM includes a lightweight portal for admin and developer self-service. This web app can integrate with your corporate single sign-on (SSO). Using the portal, operations engineers set the spend policy while developers self-provision API keys within those parameters.
  • Persistent and cache storage: LiteLLM uses Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey for non-persistent response caching. It also coordinates rate-limiting across AWS Fargate tasks. A separate Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL) database is the database of record for persistent state such as API key metadata and spend tracking.
  • Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles: Each model (such as Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku) gets its own inference profile, which you manage using the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). With this, you get per-model quota isolation and a clean abstraction layer between LiteLLM’s configuration and the model versioning of Amazon Bedrock.
  • Langfuse: Open source LLM observability for prompt-level telemetry, latency tracking, and debugging. It complements the infrastructure-level metrics of Amazon CloudWatch with application-level insight.

By using an OpenAI-compatible protocol, developers can configure their tools, such as Claude Code, Continue, and Cursor, with a single base URL and API key. Developers then operate at a level above the Amazon Bedrock backend and can swap models, add fallbacks, or migrate model providers without touching developer configurations.

Prerequisites

You will need an AWS account, Amazon Bedrock model access, and appropriate IAM permissions to deploy this project. You will also need LiteLLM. The LiteLLM AI Gateway component is open source and suitable for a small pilot with some limitations. LiteLLM documents the AI Gateway as free for up to five users with a license required beyond that. LiteLLM Enterprise is a scalable, production-minded licensed version that includes the open source gateway plus single sign-on, audit logs, delegated admin roles, and support. While the free tier supports virtual keys, the self-service key issuance described in this post requires the Enterprise version.

End-to-end configuration: Left to right

We walk through each configuration layer from the developer’s machine to the foundation model.

Step 1: Developer IDE configuration (for example, Claude Code)

Developers configure their coding assistant to point to the LLM gateway. This is the only configuration a developer needs to make to their tool:

With that configuration, each developer gets their own API key from the self-service portal and drops it into their tool configuration.

Step 2: LiteLLM gateway configuration

Deploy LiteLLM to a container service following the LiteLLM documentation. In this example we are using AWS Fargate. This will include the portal, which you can open at 

http://localhost:4000/ui
during local testing.

The LiteLLM gateway is where you will map and enforce model names to Amazon Bedrock inference profile ARNs with per-key spend limits:

Set on the Fargate task from AWS Secrets Manager:

Note: Don’t hardcode the 

master_key
or database credentials in 
config.yaml
. LiteLLM resolves 
os.environ/VAR_NAME
references at load time, so set 
LITELLM_MASTER_KEY
and 
DATABASE_URL
as environment variables on the Fargate task, sourced from AWS Secrets Manager. Set the Langfuse credentials the same way in Step 5.

When a developer calls 

claude-sonnet-4-20250514
, for example, LiteLLM resolves it to the inference profile ARN. It then authenticates to Amazon Bedrock using the AWS Fargate task’s IAM role and streams the response back in OpenAI format.

Step 3: Bedrock inference profiles (CDK)

With Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles you can create named endpoints for specific models, so you get quota isolation and fine-grained IAM control.

Choosing cross-Region inference (CRIS): Geographic or Global

Amazon Bedrock CRIS avoids the overhead of implementing cross-Region request routing yourself. Other benefits include:

  • Access to a broader pool of Regional capacity.
  • Automatic routing of requests to a supported Region with available capacity.
  • Broader model selection, because some models are available only through an inference profile.

For this proxy pattern, we recommend Global cross-Region inference when the selected models support it and organizational policies permit inference processing across supported AWS commercial Regions worldwide. Geographic cross-Region inference keeps processing within a defined geography. For example, a US inference profile routes requests only to supported US Regions. Global cross-Region inference provides access to a broader pool of Regional capacity with potential pricing benefits compared with Geographic cross-Region inference. You can verify model availability, applicable service quotas, and model-specific pricing through current AWS documentation and AWS pricing pages.

CDK construct

Important: For Global CRIS, the 

copyFrom
ARN must reference the system-defined inference profile prefixed with 
global.
, not the foundation-model ARN directly. Using a foundation-model ARN creates a single-Region profile without cross-Region routing. Additionally, the IAM policy must include the resource ARNs the invocation actually touches: the application inference profile and the underlying foundation model in any Region it might route to (Region-wildcarded). Scoping only to the application-inference-profile ARN returns 
not authorized to perform: bedrock:InvokeModel on resource: arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1::foundation-model/...
at invoke time. This is scoped least-privilege: it names the exact models in use, not 
bedrock:*
or 
*
.

Step 4: Bedrock invokes the foundation model

The inference profile handles model resolution and cross-Region routing transparently without additional configuration. When LiteLLM calls the inference profile ARN, Amazon Bedrock routes to available capacity across configured AWS Regions and returns the response.

Step 5: Langfuse observability

LiteLLM integrates with Langfuse through logging callbacks, providing visibility into model invocations without requiring changes to developer tool configurations. To enable the integration, merge the following entries into the existing litellm_settings block from the Step 2 configuration, preserving existing callback entries:

Configure the Langfuse public key, secret key, and deployment endpoint as environment variables on the Fargate task. Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager:

The endpoint must match the selected Langfuse Cloud region or self-hosted deployment. Choose the hosting option based on data governance and operational requirements. Before enabling prompt and response logging, review the content captured by the integration and configure appropriate redaction, retention, and access controls.

Langfuse traces can include prompts, responses, model parameters, token usage, and latency, depending on the integration and logging configuration. This information helps investigate unexpected model responses and complements the operational metrics collected in Amazon CloudWatch.

Implementing cost controls

Cost controls are an important dimension to a successful AI strategy. Without cost controls, heavy usage of extended thinking features can lead to unexpectedly high charges, which we observed in our early pilots.

The spend limits configured in Step 2 (

max_budget: 250
, 
budget_duration: 7d
) enforce a rolling 7-day window per API key, provided per-model 
model_info
costs are set (refer to the Step 2 note). When a user reaches their limit, LiteLLM returns an HTTP 
429
code with a clear message explaining that their budget has been exceeded. There’s no silent degradation or surprise bill. Developers and engineering teams can check current spend and reset timing through any of the following:
  • Daily spend: Query GET /user/daily/activity with a 
    start_date
    and 
    end_date
    range to get per-day metrics: spend, prompt tokens, completion tokens, and API requests, broken down by model, provider, and API key.
  • Per user spend: Query GET /user/info?user_id=… for a summary of a user’s total spend and the spend on each of their associated API keys.
  • Portal dashboard: The Admin UI (at 
    https:///ui
    ) includes a Usage tab where developers and admins can browse spend by model, user, and tag without hitting the API directly.

These same endpoints are how your finance team gets per-user attribution without you building custom metering infrastructure. A scheduled job hitting 

/user/daily/activity
or 
/global/spend/report
is enough to feed a cost dashboard or chargeback report.

Developer self-service portal

The self-service portal also handles key lifecycle processes. Developers authenticate with your corporate SSO to generate a key bound to their identity, which they can later regenerate if the key is exposed or to match a rotation policy. Platform engineers configure the budget policy once for individual developers to autonomously operate within their constraints. Two things developers use the portal for directly:

  • Key generation: On the Admin UI’s Virtual Keys page (
    https:///ui
    ), developers authenticated through SSO choose Generate Key to create their own key, bound to their identity.
  • Rate limit visibility: Each 
    /chat/completions
    response includes 
    x-litellm-key-remaining-requests-{model}
    and 
    x-litellm-key-remaining-tokens-{model}
    headers, so developers can see their remaining RPM and TPM headroom for that model directly in their tool’s response. This is distinct from the dollar-based spend tracking earlier in this post.

Monitoring and observability

For an LLM gateway, traditional metrics like latency percentiles can be misleading, especially with extended thinking models, where a single request can take several minutes. Instead, we focus on requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM) as primary signals. Here, Amazon CloudWatch can help you monitor and alarm for these signals with the following configuration.

Amazon CloudWatch alarms for quota management

Note that the alarm configuration alerts at 60–70 percent quota utilization rather than waiting for throttling. This provides lead time to scale Amazon Bedrock quotas before users experience degradation.

Emitting the metric: LiteLLM has no built-in callback that publishes a metric named 

TokensPerMinute
to a 
LiteLLM/Gateway
namespace, so the alarm needs a source. A small custom-logger callback that calls CloudWatch 
PutMetricData
on each request does the job. Register it through 
litellm_settings.success_callback
(which is additive), not 
callbacks
. The 
callbacks
list replaces LiteLLM’s internal logger list, which includes the built-in spend-tracking logger, and will silently disable budget enforcement.

Here’s a minimal version of that callback, using LiteLLM’s 

CustomLogger
class:

For prompt-level debugging, we run Langfuse alongside CloudWatch. When a developer reports “the model gave a bad response,” you can use Langfuse to inspect the exact prompt, token counts, and model parameters. For compliance-sensitive environments, Amazon Bedrock’s native invocation logging to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) provides an immutable audit trail.

Lessons learned at scale

We deployed this pattern end-to-end on a fresh AWS account to confirm the sample snippets work. In our own deployment, we scaled this LLM gateway to several hundred developers and learned several lessons.

Operational lessons

The main findings from running at scale:

  • Extended thinking changes everything about latency. Requests using Claude’s extended thinking can take several minutes or longer, depending on the thinking budget. If your load balancer has a 60-second idle timeout, those requests will fail silently. To address that, you can set load balancer idle timeouts to at least 900 seconds and configure LiteLLM’s request timeout accordingly (
    timeout: 900
    in the Step 2 configuration earlier in this post).
