  • When throttled, back off and retry on the same model before initiating a fallback. Our initial instinct was to fall back from Sonnet to Haiku upon throttling. But this is suboptimal for coding assistants because changing models breaks the consistent behavior developers rely on. Instead, retry the same model with exponential backoff at the proxy level (
    max_retries: 3
    in Step 2). When a request cannot be served after retries, surface the error clearly rather than returning an alternate model’s completions.
  • Separate automation tool invocations from developer traffic. continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines and automated code review tools should call Amazon Bedrock directly with their own inference profiles and quotas. Mixing automation traffic with interactive developer traffic leads to unpredictable latency and hinders meaningful cost attribution.
  • Start with Global CRIS from day one, if feasible. We initially used Geographic (US) CRIS but ultimately migrated our inference profiles when we reached Regional quota limits. For our use case, we didn’t have data residency constraints so we could use Global CRIS. Global CRIS routes requests across Regions to draw on a broader capacity pool, simplifying management at scale.

Deployment considerations

Two configuration mistakes are common and hard to notice until spend or connectivity breaks:

Configuring per-model costs is mandatory for enforcing budgets. The 

model_info
block on each model isn’t optional if you want to track per-user cost controls. When 
model
points at an Amazon Bedrock inference-profile ARN, LiteLLM can’t look up the ARN in its built-in pricing table. It instead records $0 per token, so the 
max_budget
and 
429
throttle enforcement silently don’t trigger. Spend remains at $0 no matter how many tokens flow. Fix this by setting 
input_cost_per_token
and 
output_cost_per_token
(or 
input_cost_per_million_tokens
).

Database compared to cache: The 

database_url
must be PostgreSQL. LiteLLM’s virtual keys (
/key/generate
), 
store_model_in_db
, and spend tracking are Postgres-backed.

A handful of smaller deployment details rounded out our checklist:

  • Global CRIS IAM needs the foundation-model resources, not only the app-inference-profile ARN. Otherwise, invocation is denied at runtime.
  • Give the Fargate task enough memory. LiteLLM’s gateway image runs out of memory and is killed at 512 MB (exit 137) before it can pass a health check. About 2 GB is a safe floor.
  • Override the container 
    entryPoint
    . The official image’s entrypoint is 
    litellm
    . If you render a config at startup with a shell script, set 
    entryPoint: ['/bin/sh','-c']
    or your script is passed as arguments to 
    litellm
    .
  • IAM role and security-group descriptions must be ASCII. Em-dashes and 
    ->
    arrows are rejected by IAM and Amazon EC2.
  • Confirm model availability in your account and Region. Model IDs and CRIS profiles change. Verify with 
    aws bedrock list-inference-profiles
    (for example, we used 
    claude-haiku-4-5
    because 
    claude-haiku-3-5
    was not available).

Clean up

This post walks through the pattern with illustrative snippets rather than a single deployable stack, there’s no one-command teardown. But the architecture relies on several resources that continue to bill while they run. These include the AWS Fargate service, Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL), Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey, and the Application Load Balancer, along with supporting Secrets Manager secrets, CloudWatch alarms, and Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles. When you finish testing, remove them to avoid ongoing charges.

If you deployed the full solution using the Guidance for Multi-Provider Generative AI Gateway on AWS, follow that solution’s cleanup instructions to remove everything it created. For AWS CDK, run cdk destroy. For AWS CloudFormation, delete the stack.

If you built the pattern yourself from the snippets in this post, remove each resource:

  • AWS Fargate service and cluster: Delete the Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) service to stop and drain the tasks, then delete the cluster.
  • Application Load Balancer: Delete the ALB along with its listeners and target groups.
  • Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL): Delete the database instance. Take a final snapshot first only if you need to retain API key and spend data.
  • Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey: Delete the replication group or cluster. It holds only cache data, so no snapshot is needed.
  • Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles: Delete the profiles created in Step 3, either by removing the AWS CDK construct or by running 
    aws bedrock delete-inference-profile
    .
  • AWS Secrets Manager secrets: Schedule deletion of the proxy’s secrets, such as the master key and database credentials.
  • Amazon CloudWatch alarms and log groups: Delete the TPM alarm and any LiteLLM log groups.

Delete the AWS Fargate service and ALB before the Amazon RDS and ElastiCache endpoints they depend on, so running tasks don’t error against removed backends during teardown.

Conclusion

In this post, we detailed a pattern for an LLM gateway that abstracts the multi-model architecture of Amazon Bedrock to provide your teams with scalable and observable self-service access. Because Amazon Bedrock routes across models through a single interface without changing infrastructure, your developers get instant access to foundation models through familiar APIs. Cost governance, observability, and a single control plane go to your engineering and security teams while finance gets per-user attribution without you building a custom metering infrastructure.

Start by working through the pattern and snippets in this post to understand how the pieces fit together. The AWS CDK snippets cover the Amazon Bedrock application inference profile, its IAM policy, and the CloudWatch alarm. The surrounding AWS Fargate service, Amazon RDS, Amazon ElastiCache, ALB, and AWS Secrets Manager resources follow standard AWS CDK patterns and aren’t shown.

When you’re ready for a complete, deployable implementation, the Guidance for Multi-Provider Generative AI Gateway on AWS closely aligns with this pattern. You can find the guide on the AWS Solutions Library with the accompanying blog post and GitHub projects. While this post stepped through the same core pattern, it focused on Amazon Bedrock for developer coding assistants. The larger solution architecture adds multi-provider support, Amazon ECS or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon CloudFront and AWS WAF options, and an admin UI.

Explore the components of this architecture with additional documentation for Amazon Bedrock Inference Profiles, LiteLLM gateway, AWS Fargate, and Langfuse.

Try this pattern in your organization. Start with a pilot team, validate the cost controls, and scale from there.

entries.title: Run agents securely and efficiently with the next generation AgentCore runtime
entries.summary: AI agents now run multi-step workloads for hours and act on behalf of users, raising the bar for secure, scalable agent compute. Learn how the next generation of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime delivers hardware-isolated sessions with faster starts, more compute, usage-based billing, and isolation that now extends to your data.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Run agents securely and efficiently with the next generation AgentCore runtime

AI agents have moved past one-off prompts. They now run multi-step workloads for hours at a time. The length of task that frontier agents can complete on their own doubles about every four months (METR), and 40 percent of large enterprises are scaling AI agents, up from 27 percent a year ago (McKinsey). As agents run longer and with more autonomy, the focus shifts from what agents can do to how securely, reliably, and economically they can operate at scale. Agents do more than traditional software: they execute code, navigate browsers, access sensitive data, and act on behalf of users. These capabilities introduce new security and infrastructure demands, making strong isolation essential for production deployments.

Every agent session needs a secure, isolated environment. But delivering that isolation at scale introduces a fundamental challenge: balancing performance, cost, and efficiency. Pre-provisioned environments consume resources even when idle, driving up costs. On-demand environments reduce wasted capacity but introduce cold-start latency, delaying agent execution. Neither approach scales efficiently without trade-offs. As organizations move from deploying a handful of agents to running thousands of concurrent sessions, building and managing custom sandboxes becomes increasingly complex, expensive, and unpredictable.

The challenge is evident. Only 15 percent of organizations have scaled orchestrated, multi-agent systems, and 70 percent say they can’t yet trust and govern their agents (Deloitte). Scaling agents shouldn’t mean choosing between security, speed, and cost. The next generation of agent infrastructure must deliver strong isolation with fast startup times, elastic scaling, and usage-based economics. Because as AI agents move into production, secure execution shouldn’t be the bottleneck. It should be the foundation that makes scale possible. The fastest path to production should also be the safest one.

The next generation AgentCore runtime

We built Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to help developers build, connect, and optimize agents securely at scale. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is the managed compute layer. It gives developers a fully managed environment to deploy and run agents without building or maintaining infrastructure. Since launching, our customers have been pushing their agents into increasingly complex workloads. As those workloads grow, so do the demands on the execution environment: more compute, more flexible billing, and trust boundaries that extend to data, not only compute. Agents reach production at scale if the infrastructure underneath was built for both scale and speed.

Today we’re announcing updates to AgentCore runtime that meet those demands. The core guarantee stands: every session runs in its own hardware-isolated Firecracker micro virtual machine (MicroVM), with its own identity, policy, and audit trail. These updates expand what’s possible within that guarantee. Sessions now start up to 15x faster, scale to 4x more compute, and run up to 68% more efficiently, with the isolation boundary fully intact.

Here’s what’s new.

Run bigger workloads without waiting longer to start

Teams building increasingly advanced agents asked for more flexibility: the ability to scale memory and compute within the isolated session to match the demands of their workloads. From large codebase compilations to browser-driven workflows to local model inference, the execution environment needs to keep pace.

Sessions now scale 4x compared to the previous version, up to 8 vCPUs and 32 GB, with support for container images up to 10 GB. Sessions start in under 2 seconds, independent of image size and concurrency. You no longer need warm pools and pre-provisioned clusters to manage cold starts.

“AgentCore Runtime lets us run AI-driven development at scale. Each coding agent session runs in its own hardware-isolated environment, which we need when agents execute code, and the runtime scales elastically with demand and starts fast every time, so our engineers move quickly without managing any infrastructure.”

— Siwei Shen, VP of Engineering, Coinbase

“Mission is using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime to power a natural-language query agent that helps users retrieve property and sales insights without navigating complex data systems. In our initial comparison of both runtime versions, the same workload delivered 35% faster cold starts for inference requests and 77% faster starts for health checks, while reducing measured runtime cost per call by 17%. The new AgentCore runtime gives us a compelling combination of faster agent experiences and more efficient resource utilization as we bring enterprise agents into production.”

— Dr. Ryan Ries, Chief AI & Data Scientist, Mission Cloud

“Our approach is to run Zuora’s cloud with automation and AI agents wherever we can, and that only works if the runtime is efficient and reliable. The next generation AgentCore runtime cut our memory footprint per invocation by around 60% in many use cases while handling more traffic at steady latency. That gives us a stronger cost profile as we expand agentic workloads across our platform.”

— Brad Ruppert, VP of Cloud and Security, Zuora

“The Rescale platform helps R&D and engineering teams accelerate product development with agentic digital engineering. Our engineering-specific agents validate simulation inputs, troubleshoot jobs, select hardware, and generate reports, while engineers stay in control. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime allows us to deploy and scale those agents in production without building or operating the underlying agent infrastructure, so we can deliver new agents to customers faster.”

— Mark Whitney, VP Engineering, Rescale

Stop paying for idle agents

As teams move agents closer to production, they asked for billing that reflects how agents actually work. Agents spend much of their time waiting on a model response, a tool call, or a human decision. Agents should be billed for the work they do, not the time they spend waiting.

The runtime now reclaims memory within minutes of the agent releasing it, and an idle agent scales to zero. For multi-turn agents with natural pauses between interactions, this means up to 68 percent less memory consumed per session. For always-on agents, committed baseline pricing sets a memory baseline per session, billed as a minimum, with room to burst up to four times that baseline on demand. This gives steady workloads a predictable rate at AWS Lambda MicroVM rates. The runtime uses compute more efficiently, so you pay less for the same work. That makes the finance conversation that often gates production rollouts easier to close.

“The next generation Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime helps us deliver more responsive AI experiences by starting agents faster and using memory more efficiently. Aligning consumption with actual usage gives our clients great confidence to scale agentic solutions while keeping costs connected to real demand.”

— Ashwin Patil, Principal, AI and Data Leader, Deloitte Consulting LLP

“AgentCore runtime gives us a managed foundation for building agentic products and platforms around our customers’ data, tools, and business processes. The next generation Agentcore runtime makes that foundation more responsive and resource-efficient by restoring initialized environments and reclaiming unused memory. We’re beginning to build on the latest version because the cost and latency reductions make a significant difference in how our customers’ businesses operate.”

— Randall Hunt, CTO, Caylent

Isolation now extends to your data

Many enterprises face a persistent gap in their agent security model. The agent runs inside an isolated session, but the data it requires resides outside that boundary. Long-running agents pick up context as they go: files, credentials, tool outputs, and more. Teams end up building their own rules for how data moves in and out, adding complexity and risk with every new agent.

Isolation that stops at compute is only half a boundary. The next generation AgentCore runtime closes that gap. Each session still runs in its own hardware-isolated environment with its own identity, access policy, and audit trail. Agents can now dynamically mount and save their work to a filesystem, such as an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket with FUSE support. Your data stays inside the trust boundary for the entire job, governed by a single set of controls you define once.

“At Okta, the combination of AgentCore runtime and Lambda MicroVMs provide the isolated execution environment and contextual memory our agents need to inspect code, run test suites, and open pull requests within ephemeral sandboxes. Paired with our identity-governed policy controls, AgentCore Runtime and Lambda MicroVMs demonstrate how we can safely scale autonomous engineering agents without risking workspace leakage or privilege escalation.”

— Monica Bajaj, SVP Engineering, Okta

“From helping car shoppers value a trade-in to helping dealers book service appointments and structure deals, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore powers dozens of agentic solutions across Cox Automotive’s brands. Having a single, governed agent platform lets our teams across our business move from pilot to production with confidence.”

— Chris Dillon, VP, Product and Engineering, Cox Automotive

“With the next generation of CoCounsel Legal, we set out to build an agentic system that does more than answer questions: it works through a matter end to end, from research to trusted work product. Getting that into customers’ hands quickly meant spending our time on legal reasoning and quality, rather than on running agent infrastructure. With AgentCore Runtime handling the hosting and scaling, we moved from prototype to production fast and kept complete control over how our agents operate and integrate with our existing systems. Our developers build on their preferred frameworks, and Runtime gives us the enterprise-grade reliability and isolation we need to run CoCounsel’s agentic legal workflows at scale for legal professionals around the world.”

— Danilo Tommasina, Distinguished Engineer – Thomson Reuters

Our commitment

The agents that reach production are the ones you trust to act on your behalf, with real data, real stakes, and real accountability. Trust isn’t a feature you add later. It’s the runtime you build on. This release is a step toward that future: bigger sessions, efficient resource use, and storage inside the trust boundary, without loosening the isolation that makes the work trustworthy. By re:Invent, per-session scoping will bind each session to its own storage folder through session-labeled credentials, and we will keep building from there.

Get started

The next generation AgentCore runtime is available today in AWS Regions across North America, South America, Europe, and Asia Pacific. Visit Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to build on it or open the Amazon Bedrock console to start exploring.

entries.title: Migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with your coding agent
entries.summary: The migration guide in the amazon-bedrock skill helps you migrate a customer-managed Amazon Bedrock knowledge base to a Managed Knowledge Base. Your coding agent plans the move with read-only discovery, creates the new knowledge base or an infrastructure-as-code template alongside the original, and validates retrieval before you cut over.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with your coding agent

With a customer-managed knowledge base on Amazon Bedrock, you provision and scale the vector store, tune the embedding model and index settings, and plan capacity for each new data source. The migration guide in the Agent Toolkit for AWS helps you migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base. Managed Knowledge Base takes over that work and adds new retrieval capabilities, and your team keeps control of the content and the application that uses it.

Moving a production knowledge base means your team maps its configuration, creates the replacement, ingests content, updates the application’s retrieval call, and validates retrieval before switching traffic. To help, we added a knowledge base migration guide to the 

amazon-bedrock
skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS. The guide gives your coding agent the context to plan the migration with you, starting with read-only discovery and a plan you review line by line. On your approval, the agent creates the new knowledge base and its data sources alongside the original, or writes a migrated infrastructure as code (IaC) template for your pipeline. Ingestion and updating your application’s 
Retrieve
calls stay with you, and your agent can walk you through both.

In this post, we explain why we recommend the move and how the migration guide works, review the prerequisites, install the skill, plan a migration, update the application’s retrieval call, and validate retrieval before cutover.

Why move to Managed Knowledge Base

We recommend Managed Knowledge Base because it balances ease of use, retrieval accuracy, and cost.

AWS runs the store

With a Managed Knowledge Base, Amazon Bedrock handles ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval, and the store scales automatically as your content grows. Hybrid search, which combines keyword and semantic matching, is always on, with no index to configure. The knowledge base includes a managed embedding model, a managed reranker, and a built-in parser for multimodal file types.

You can still bring your own Amazon Bedrock embedding model when you create the knowledge base. On each retrieval request, you choose the managed reranker, an Amazon Bedrock reranking model, or no reranking. The managed reranker requires the managed embedding model.

Built-in capabilities

Managed Knowledge Base includes capabilities you’d otherwise build yourself:

  • Native connectors ingest content directly from sources such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Microsoft SharePoint, and Atlassian Confluence. For the current list, see supported connectors. After the first full sync, later syncs pick up only changes, on demand or on a schedule. The Managed Knowledge Base includes a deletion safeguard to help protect against accidental bulk removal of indexed content.
  • Access control list (ACL) awareness ingests document permissions with the content, so retrieval returns only what the signed-in user can access. For connectors that support it, such as Microsoft SharePoint and Atlassian Confluence, a real-time check against the source also catches permission changes since the last sync. ACL awareness doesn’t authenticate users, so your application must verify and pass the user’s identity.
  • Agentic retrieval answers questions that a single search can’t by handling multi-part questions and retrieving iteratively. It can search more than one knowledge base in a single request.
  • Integration with AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, exposes your knowledge base as a target. Any client that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) can then query the knowledge base, and the gateway handles authentication.
  • Resource-based policies let applications in other AWS accounts use one team’s knowledge base. Scope each policy to the specific roles that call the knowledge base, and grant only the actions they use, such as 
    bedrock:Retrieve
    .

Agentic retrieval, AgentCore Gateway integration, and resource-based policies are not available on customer-managed knowledge bases. For the AWS Regions where managed knowledge bases are available, and the features that AWS GovCloud (US-West) doesn’t support, see Supported AWS Regions.

Higher quotas

As of this writing, higher default quotas change how you can organize content. With 200 data sources per knowledge base, you can group related content in one knowledge base. With 10,000 knowledge bases per account, per Region, each team or product line can use a separate knowledge base.

Default quotaCustomer-managedManaged
Knowledge bases per account, per Region10010,000
Data sources per knowledge base5200
Concurrent ingestion jobs per knowledge base150
Query input characters1,00010,000

For current values, see Amazon Bedrock endpoints and quotas and Service quotas for managed knowledge bases.

Pay for what you store and retrieve

Cost is one of three things teams weigh when they consider this move, alongside customizability and direct control of the vector store. On a customer-managed knowledge base, you choose, provision, scale, and update the vector and text stores, and pay separately for the infrastructure you select. On a Managed Knowledge Base, those stages are part of the service, and storage and retrieval are metered directly.

The pricing models can differ too. With a customer-managed knowledge base, storage and retrieval charges depend on the vector store you choose. Some stores charge for provisioned or minimum capacity, and others, such as Amazon S3 Vectors, a capability of Amazon S3, charge only for what you use. A Managed Knowledge Base is priced on what you store and retrieve, so cost follows real usage. Usage-based pricing can fit enterprise question-answering, policy, and support knowledge bases that run at low utilization. For current rates, see Amazon Bedrock pricing. For the parsers available on a customer-managed knowledge base and how each is billed, see Parsing options for your data source.

Cost driverCustomer-managed knowledge baseManaged Knowledge Base
Vector storagePriced separately by your chosen store. A provisioned retrieval service can have a minimum idle cost even at low volumeIncluded in the base storage rate of $5 per GB per month
Multimodal document parsingRequires Amazon Bedrock Data Automation, billed by page or image, or a foundation model, billed by token. Text-only parsing is free.Included
Embedding generationBilled separately at your embedding model’s rateIncluded with the default model. Charges apply only if you choose a custom model
Ingestion, sync, and re-sync computeRe-embedding, orchestration code, and indexing compute spikes on each sync add recurring costIncluded, with incremental sync that processes only new and changed content
ConnectorsBuilding and running custom connectors can add compute costNative connectors are included
Standard retrievalNo Amazon Bedrock charge per query. Your vector store can charge per query, as Amazon S3 Vectors does.$1 per 1,000 retrieval requests
RerankingAmazon Rerank is charged at $1 per 1,000 queries. A custom reranking model is billed at its own rateIncluded in the $1 per 1,000 retrieval requests
Agentic retrievalYou build the agentic workflow on a Bedrock model, which can cost roughly $18 to $24 per 1,000 queries before development and maintenance. Because model usage is billed by token, the price per query varies.Agentic retrieval costs an additional $4 per 1,000 queries on top of the underlying retrieval calls, including multi-shot retrieval, reranking, and answer generation. Depending on the number of underlying retrieval calls, the total can range from roughly $6 to $9 per 1,000 queries.

Rates are only part of the total cost of ownership. On a customer-managed knowledge base, your team provisions, scales, and operates each stage as a separate resource. A Managed Knowledge Base consolidates them into one resource, with a default embedding model, foundation model, and reranker, and with per-knowledge-base rate limits by default. You manage the content and the application that uses it, and Amazon Bedrock operates the managed storage, embedding model, foundation model, and reranker.

Solution overview

A customer-managed knowledge base uses the 

VECTOR
type, with a vector store you configure. A Managed Knowledge Base uses the 
MANAGED
type. The migration guide directs your agent to create a new 
MANAGED
knowledge base alongside the original without modifying or deleting the original during migration. Using the guide’s map, your agent writes a plan that lists which settings remain unchanged, which Managed handles differently, and which application changes you need to make. As Figure 1 shows, the original keeps serving every request while your team ingests content, validates, and cuts over.

How the migration guide works

The guide separates planning from implementation. In Explore mode, your agent answers questions about Managed Knowledge Base and can inspect your configuration with read-only calls, so you can estimate the effort. In Migration mode, the guide takes your agent through checkpoints:

  • Introduce and choose. Your agent explains what it will and won’t touch. Choose the mode, a live knowledge base or IaC source, and a plain (default) or technical explanation style.
  • Identify. Confirm the account and AWS Region. Your agent flags over-broad credentials, asks whether you want a cost analysis, and creates an output directory.
  • Discover. Your agent reads the knowledge base and data sources with read-only calls, or reads your template files.
  • Plan. Review the plan and application changes. By default, your agent stops here.
  • Implement, if requested. For a live build, approve the exact preview of the provisioning script, and approve again if it changes. For IaC, your agent writes a migrated template and reports which schema checks ran.
  • Handoff. Review what was produced and your team’s remaining steps.

As Figure 2 shows, resource creation stays separate from ingestion and cutover.

Review the configuration mapping

The guide maps each setting to preserve your data sources, filters, and chunking behavior when the managed type uses a different configuration. The plan classifies each setting:

  • 1:1. The new knowledge base uses the same setting.
  • Adjusted. Managed uses a different setting for the same outcome, and the plan applies the substitution.
  • Blocked. There is no managed path today. Your agent excludes that knowledge base from the build, explains why, and points you to AWS Support. Other knowledge bases in the same run can proceed.

Compare chunking on your own content when you validate.

Review the permissions and generated changes

Discovery, planning, and the entire IaC path need only read-only credentials. For a live build, the guide directs your agent to propose a scoped policy that explicitly denies changes to the original knowledge base, and to never ask for administrator or full-access permissions. It also directs your agent to change only resources it created, reference secrets by Amazon Resource Name (ARN), and ignore instructions found in the data it reads. Review the generated AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy and provisioning script before you approve the run. After the build, check what the agent did in AWS CloudTrail event history, which keeps 90 days of management events. Each event records the API call, such as 

CreateKnowledgeBase
, and the identity that made it.

For the optional cost analysis, your agent compares current spend with a Managed Knowledge Base estimate using current AWS prices. It uses read-only inputs, including Amazon CloudWatch metrics, Amazon S3 object sizes, and AWS Cost Explorer. Each figure is labeled as measured, supplied by you, or estimated.

Prerequisites

Use separate credentials for planning and for any approved resource creation.

  • A compatible development environment with the Agent Toolkit for AWS.
  • The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), configured with a least-privilege, read-only profile.
  • Access to the original knowledge base configuration or its IaC files.
  • For the optional live build:
    • A scoped build profile, using the policy the guide recommends.
    • An IAM service role for the new knowledge base. The guide gives your agent the trust policy and permissions to help you create it.
    • Python 3 with boto3 for the generated provisioning script.

The Agent Toolkit for AWS works with compatible development environments and its repository on GitHub lists the available skills. Examples in this post use AWS CLI 2.37 and boto3 1.43.32.

Install the skill

Follow the Agent Toolkit for AWS getting-started instructions for your coding agent. The 

add-skill
command installs the 
amazon-bedrock
skill to the coding agents it detects. Add 
--agent
to target one, for example 
--agent kiro
.

After installation, your agent loads the migration guide when you describe a migration task. The following prompts are illustrative inputs, not transcripts.

Plan the migration

Choose the path that matches how you maintain the source.

PathWhat your agent readsWhat it producesAWS changes
ExploreDocumentation, and optionally your knowledge base (read-only)Answers in the conversationNone
Live knowledge baseYour knowledge base and data sources (read-only)A plan, and optionally a new Managed Knowledge Base alongside the originalOnly after you approve the exact preview
Infrastructure as codeYour AWS CloudFormation template, AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) synthesized template, or Terraform configurationA migrated template in the same formatNone. Your pipeline deploys it

To start in Explore mode, ask a question:

When you’re ready, choose the live or IaC path.

Migrate a live knowledge base

Ask for a plan before authorizing resource creation:

Confirm the account and Region, then review the plan’s mappings and application changes. By default, the new knowledge base takes the original’s name with a 

-managed
suffix. To build it, confirm the service role exists, switch to the build profile, inspect the provisioning script and its preview, and approve. Your agent runs the script, which creates the knowledge base and data sources, and reports their status.

Migrate infrastructure as code

Point your agent at the source template or configuration:

Your agent writes the migrated file to the output directory, deploys nothing, and shows you the diff. To keep the diff, ask your agent to save it. Run 

terraform init -backend=false
and 
terraform validate
before deployment. Your agent can walk you through both commands, but the guide leaves these checks to you because 
terraform init
downloads the large AWS provider. Before you apply the deployment plan, check that it keeps the original resources you need for rollback.

Example conversation

The migration runs as a conversation. Before reading anything, your agent states its scope and asks how to proceed:

The plan summary shows each mapping, the caller changes, and the decisions you need to make:

For a live build, your agent stops at a preview, and the approval command requires the plan’s hash:

Example exchanges are lightly edited, with identifiers replaced.

Update the application’s retrieval call

Your application uses the same 

Retrieve
operation for both types. The managed request targets the new knowledge base ID and replaces 
vectorSearchConfiguration
with 
managedSearchConfiguration
. Passing 
vectorSearchConfiguration
to a managed knowledge base returns a validation error. Managed retrieval always uses hybrid search, so the managed request shape has no 
overrideSearchType
field. Metadata filters keep the same syntax, except that managed knowledge bases don’t support the 
startsWith
and 
stringContains
operators. For the full syntax, see the Retrieve API reference.

The example assumes both knowledge bases contain the 

locale
metadata used by the filter.

Validate retrieval and cut over

Evaluate the new knowledge base while the application still uses the original.

  • If using IaC, review and deploy the target configuration through your pipeline.
  • Sync each data source and review any failures. See Sync your data.
  • Grant your application’s runtime IAM role 
    bedrock:Retrieve
    on the new knowledge base ARN, and keep its access to the original knowledge base so you can roll back.
  • Run representative queries against both knowledge bases with 
    Retrieve
    , using that role. The two types use different score scales. Managed scores also depend on 
    rerankingModelType
    , which defaults to 
    MANAGED
    with the managed embedding model and to 
    NONE
    with a custom one. Tune thresholds per mode, and hold the mode constant while comparing.
  • Test metadata filters and permission-aware retrieval where used, including content the signed-in user shouldn’t receive. On an ACL-enabled data source, requests without 
    userContext.userId
    (the user’s email) return no results.
  • After acceptance, deploy the new knowledge base ID and request shape. Keep the original knowledge base, with current content, and application configuration through your rollback period.

For each query, check whether both return the same top document and how much results overlap. A short script can report pass or fail against criteria such as a matching top document on at least 90 percent of queries and no zero-result queries on the managed knowledge base. Tune that threshold for your workload. For other retrieval quality measures, such as context relevance and context coverage, see Use metrics to understand RAG system performance.

Watch for these differences when you compare results:

  • Normalize source locations before comparison. A customer-managed knowledge base can return 
    s3://bucket/key
    in 
    location.s3Location.uri
    , and a managed knowledge base can return an 
    https://
    URL. Compare by object key.
  • Compare the top result instead of assuming equal result counts. The two knowledge base types can return different numbers of results, and 
    numberOfResults
    sets a maximum rather than a guarantee. Compare the top document, and review each query where it changes. For details, see Configure and customize queries for managed knowledge bases.
  • Map renamed system metadata keys. For example, replace 
    x-amz-bedrock-kb-data-source-id
    with 
    _data_source_id
    in comparison code. Your own metadata attributes keep their names. For details, see Configure and customize queries for managed knowledge bases.

Clean up

If you complete the migration, retire the original only after the rollback period and a dependency review. Keep the source documents and buckets the managed knowledge base ingests from, and storage that other workloads use. Clean up IaC-managed resources through their owning template.

If you end the evaluation instead, keep the original and delete what you created in this order:

  • Delete each managed data source and wait until it’s gone.
  • Delete the managed knowledge base and wait until it’s gone.
  • If you created the service role only for this evaluation, delete its inline policy, then the role.
  • With a customer managed key, check 
    aws kms list-grants
    for grants Amazon Bedrock created, which can remain after the knowledge base is deleted.
  • Keep any S3 bucket that another knowledge base still reads.

Deletion protection on a managed data source limits how much a sync can delete, not whether you can delete the data source. Deleting the original knowledge base doesn’t delete its vector store, which continues to incur charges until you remove it. See Delete an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base.

Conclusion

With Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, your team no longer runs a vector store or manages the underlying retrieval infrastructure. With the migration guide in the 

amazon-bedrock
skill, you ask your agent for a plan, review it, and approve only the resources you want built.

To get started, set up the Agent Toolkit for AWS and ask your agent for a read-only assessment of your knowledge base. After migration, explore agentic retrieval for multi-part questions. To learn more, see Build enterprise search for agents with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base on the AWS Machine Learning Blog.

entries.title: Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS
entries.summary: Build a composable, interoperable multi-agent system on AWS with the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol. A LangChain orchestrator on Amazon ECS communicates with a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore across organizational boundaries, using bidirectional, OAuth-authenticated calls, with neither side depending on the other's framework or SDK.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS

Agents in multi-agent systems that span organizational boundaries often need to collaborate in a composable, interoperable way, with agents that other organizations build and run. They need a way to discover each other, communicate, and exchange tasks without exposing internals or requiring the same framework on both sides.

The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol addresses this constraint. Without A2A, building composable multi-agent systems across organizational boundaries requires custom integration code for each customer and framework. Independent software vendors (ISVs) can instead build composable, interoperable agents that work with the A2A-compatible frameworks their customers already use.

While we frame this post around the ISV use case, the pattern also applies to organizations that expose agents across boundaries, whether to partners, customers, or internal teams that use different frameworks. As your system grows, you add skills by registering Agent Cards with the orchestrator, without changing the agents already running.

In this post, we walk through a deployed reference architecture on AWS. A LangChain-based enterprise orchestrator communicates with a Strands Agents-based software as a service (SaaS) agent across organizational boundaries using A2A, with the enterprise and the SaaS provider in separate AWS accounts. Neither side depends on the other’s framework or SDK, and the two sides share no secrets. We cover the architecture and implementation patterns, then deploy the system from three Jupyter notebooks and run an end-to-end test.

The A2A protocol is now a Linux Foundation project, and AWS is among the organizations that support it. With A2A, agents can discover each other, negotiate tasks, and collaborate across organizational boundaries through a standardized protocol. The protocol uses existing authentication standards such as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) for cross-boundary security, and is designed to work across A2A-compatible frameworks.

In Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A, we introduced A2A concepts and demonstrated two Strands agents communicating using the protocol on AWS. That post established the foundation with Agent Card discovery, structured task execution, and the A2A server pattern. This post builds on that foundation with cross-framework interoperability, cross-organizational trust boundaries, and OAuth in both directions.

Solution overview

Three agents run in two AWS accounts, one for the enterprise and one for the SaaS provider. The A2A protocol connects them, with OAuth authentication in both directions. Each account has its own Amazon Cognito user pool, so each side authenticates with its own identity provider.

During onboarding, the enterprise and the SaaS provider exchange only public values, such as identity provider URLs, client IDs, scopes, and endpoint URLs. Each side then trusts tokens from the other side’s user pool, and no secrets are shared.

After onboarding, each request follows these steps:

  • The enterprise app gets an access token from the enterprise’s Amazon Cognito user pool.
  • The app sends a question over HTTPS to the user API in Amazon API Gateway, then polls for the answer.
  • Amazon API Gateway forwards the request privately, through a VPC link and an internal Network Load Balancer, to the Enterprise Orchestrator, a LangChain agent.
  • When its model decides that the question needs a compliance scan, the orchestrator gets its own token from the enterprise user pool, using a client secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager.
  • The orchestrator sends an A2A request to the compliance SaaS agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, using the skill it read from the agent’s Agent Card at startup.
  • The compliance agent checks the enterprise context agent’s Agent Card at the callback URL registered at onboarding, then gets a token from the SaaS provider’s own pool.
  • The compliance agent calls back to the enterprise context agent for account metadata, finishes its scan, and returns the answer to the orchestrator and then to the app.

On the enterprise side, two agents run on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate. The Enterprise Orchestrator is the entry point for users. LangChain provides the agent framework and tool-calling abstractions, and Amazon Bedrock provides the foundation models (FMs) that power each agent’s reasoning. The orchestrator uses LangChain and Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6). At startup, the orchestrator fetches the SaaS agent’s Agent Card from its well-known URL and creates a LangChain tool for each skill described on the card. The model then decides which tool to call based on the user’s question, so the orchestrator needs no hardcoded routing logic. It sends compliance scan requests over A2A with OAuth bearer tokens and summarizes the results for leadership. Users reach the orchestrator through an Amazon API Gateway HTTPS endpoint that accepts only tokens from the enterprise’s own pool.

The second enterprise agent provides internal context. The Enterprise Context Agent is built with LangChain and Amazon Bedrock (Amazon Nova Lite). It provides internal account metadata such as internal policy rules, data classification, business criticality, and escalation contacts (team on-call rotations). The deployed agent uses the official a2a-sdk (AgentCard, AgentExecutor, and spec-conformant JSON-RPC routes), pinned to a2a-sdk[http-server]==1.2.2. The SaaS agent reaches the context agent through an API Gateway partner API that accepts only the SaaS provider’s callback token.

Both enterprise agents run in private subnets of an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), with no public IP addresses.

On the SaaS provider side, the Compliance SaaS Agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in the SaaS provider’s own AWS account. Built with the Strands Agents SDK, it checks AWS accounts against the enterprise’s own internal policies, such as no public storage in production and encryption at rest for confidential data. In production, the scanning tools would connect to services such as AWS Config, AWS Security Hub, or Amazon GuardDuty. For this demo, the agent uses synthetic data that simulates compliance findings across multiple accounts.

Before it scans, the SaaS agent calls back to the Enterprise Context Agent for enterprise context, such as which accounts are production, which internal policies apply, and who to escalate to. This bidirectional pattern makes the agents true peers instead of a client and a server. The callback goes only to the address the customer registered at onboarding.

The key design decision is to use A2A for all cross-boundary communication. The enterprise has no access to the SaaS agent’s internal tools, system prompt, or model choice. This separation means the ISV can change its internal architecture without changing customer integrations, as long as its Agent Card and A2A interface stay compatible. The SaaS card publishes one curated skill, not its internal tool names.

Amazon Bedrock provides API access to multiple foundation models, so each agent can use the model that fits its workload. In this solution, the orchestrator and SaaS agent use Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 for complex reasoning, while the context agent uses Amazon Nova Lite for metadata lookups. You can choose different models based on your own requirements.

A2A and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) solve different problems in this architecture. MCP connects an agent to its own tools and data sources in a client-server model. A2A connects agents to other agents as peers, where neither side exposes its internals. In production, the SaaS agent could use MCP internally to connect to its compliance scanning tools while exposing itself externally through A2A. The external interface stays the same regardless of how the agent connects to its internal tools.

Prerequisites

The notebooks contain the complete deployment procedure. Before you run them, you need the following:

  • Two AWS accounts, one for the enterprise and one for the SaaS provider, in the same AWS Region: us-east-1, us-east-2, or us-west-2. In both accounts, access to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 in Amazon Bedrock, and in the enterprise account, access to Amazon Nova Lite. Before the first run, submit the Anthropic first-time use form in each account, and give the identity you run the notebooks with the AWS Marketplace permissions listed in the Amazon Bedrock model access documentation. Model availability varies by Region. Check the Amazon Bedrock model availability documentation for the current list.
  • A Jupyter environment with Python 3.10 or later, either:
    • On your computer: JupyterLab, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) version 2, and an AWS IAM Identity Center profile for each account, set up with aws configure sso. You don’t need Docker: AWS CodeBuild builds the container images.
    • Or an Amazon SageMaker AI notebook instance in each account (ml.t3.medium is enough). See the Guide to getting set up with Amazon SageMaker AI.
  • In each account, an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role with permissions to create AWS CloudFormation stacks and the resources in them. Each notebook lists the exact permissions in its Reference section. See the IAM User Guide.

Notebook 3 also runs the end-to-end test described later in this post, so you can verify the deployment.

Running this solution incurs charges for the resources it creates. In the enterprise account, the main always-on resources are a NAT gateway, two AWS Fargate tasks, the internal Network Load Balancer, and two interface VPC endpoints. Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore charge for what you use. Prices vary by AWS Region. See the pricing pages for Amazon VPC, AWS Fargate, Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Elastic Load Balancing. Run the Clean up sections when you finish.

Implement the solution

Deploy the system with three notebooks, run in order with Jupyter, one cell at a time. Notebook 1 (enterprise account, about 3 minutes) creates the enterprise identity and writes an onboarding request. Notebook 2 (SaaS provider account, about 5 minutes) deploys the compliance agent and writes an onboarding response. Notebook 3 (enterprise account, about 20 minutes) deploys the enterprise agents and runs the tests. The onboarding files hold only public values.

  • Clone the GitHub repository, and set up two AWS profiles for local runs, or one notebook instance per account with the repository cloned to each.
  • Run notebook 1 in the enterprise account.
  • Give 
    onboarding-request.json
    to the SaaS provider.
  • Run notebook 2 in the SaaS provider account.
  • Give 
    onboarding-response.json
    back to the enterprise.
  • Run notebook 3 in the enterprise account.
  • After testing, run notebook 3’s Clean up, then notebook 2’s.

The following sections explain the key implementation patterns behind the deployment. Together, they demonstrate three capabilities:

  • Interoperability across frameworks – A LangChain orchestrator calls a Strands agent using A2A, with neither side depending on the other’s SDK.
  • Composability across organizational boundaries – An ISV’s compliance agent and an enterprise’s context agent compose into a workflow that neither team built alone.
  • Bidirectional collaboration with OAuth – Agents act as peers, calling each other across trust boundaries with token-based authentication.

With A2A, the ISV in this scenario replaces multiple custom integration paths with a single protocol-based interface.

Build the SaaS compliance agent

Build the ISV’s compliance agent with the Strands Agents SDK and deploy it to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. For this demo, the scanning tools return synthetic compliance findings.

The agent exposes three compliance tools using the Strands @tool decorator (listing available accounts, running compliance scans, and retrieving remediation steps), plus a fourth that calls back to the enterprise, covered in the next section. The Agent Card doesn’t list these tools. It publishes one curated skill, so callers’ models see what the product does, not how it’s built. This simplified example shows the scanning tool:

Enable the bidirectional callback

This is where the solution goes beyond typical agent integrations. Most agent-to-agent demos show one-way request and response, where a client agent calls a server agent and waits for the result. That pattern breaks down when the called agent needs information that only the caller has. In production, agents need to be peers that can call each other.

The SaaS compliance agent needs enterprise context. Examples include which accounts are production, which internal policies apply, and who to escalate to. This is information that only the enterprise has.

The SaaS agent calls back over A2A, but only to the callback URL the customer registered at onboarding. It first verifies the customer’s public context card there, then gets a token from the SaaS provider’s own Cognito pool, and sends message/send to the enterprise partner API:

Every failure, from an unverified card to a rejected token, gives the model one message, “Enterprise context unavailable”, and the details stay in the SaaS provider’s logs.

Expose the agent over A2A on AgentCore

The A2AServer class from the Strands SDK handles the A2A protocol, Agent Card generation, and JSON-RPC message handling. The server publishes one curated skill and declares on the card how a caller gets a token:

When deployed to AgentCore, this automatically generates an Agent Card at 

/.well-known/agent-card.json
. The Agent Card is a JSON document that describes the agent’s name, capabilities, and skills. A2A-compatible clients can fetch this card and understand what the agent can do without documentation or SDK integration.

Build the enterprise orchestrator with LangChain

This is the interoperability proof. The enterprise orchestrator uses LangChain, deliberately different from the Strands-based SaaS agent. It uses raw httpx HTTP calls with A2A JSON-RPC and doesn’t depend on the Strands SDK. If the ISV switched from Strands to another A2A-compatible framework, the enterprise orchestrator would keep working without changes, as long as the SaaS agent still speaks A2A and publishes a compatible Agent Card. That is what protocol-level interoperability means in practice.

The orchestrator gets a token from the enterprise’s own Cognito pool and sends the JSON-RPC payload over HTTPS only to the agent URL pinned to the address it fetched the Agent Card from. This abridged code shows the core A2A client:

Discover agents and route requests with the LLM

At startup, the orchestrator fetches Agent Cards from configured ISV URLs. It reads the skill descriptions from each card and creates a LangChain tool for each skill. The orchestrator’s large language model (LLM), Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, then decides which tool to call based on the user’s question. This simplified code shows the pattern:

As a result, when the ISV adds or changes a capability, its Agent Card changes with it, and the orchestrator picks up the new skills the next time it restarts. The two teams don’t need to coordinate the change.

Build the enterprise context agent

The enterprise context agent uses LangChain and Amazon Nova Lite for enterprise metadata lookups, and exposes its capabilities over A2A using the official a2a-sdk. The SDK handles Agent Card serving, JSON-RPC routing, and protocol conformance. Because A2A is JSON-RPC over HTTP, a standard web framework can serve it. The orchestrator shows the client side: it sends A2A requests with plain httpx and no A2A SDK.

The agent also publishes its own Agent Card at 

/.well-known/agent-card.json
, which the SaaS agent checks before it calls back. This is the same discovery mechanism used in the other direction. The A2A specification defines Agent Cards, so they don’t depend on the framework that builds the agent.

Set up cross-boundary OAuth with Amazon Cognito

Agent-to-agent communication across organizational boundaries without authentication isn’t acceptable to most enterprises. Every A2A task request (message/send) in this solution carries a JSON Web Token (JWT). Each side authenticates with a token from its own identity provider, and the receiving side accepts only that provider, one client, and one scope. The only unauthenticated endpoint is the enterprise context agent’s Agent Card, which publishes descriptive metadata so callers can discover the agent.

The solution uses Amazon Cognito as the OAuth provider. The same pattern can use another OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider that issues signed JWT access tokens, after you update the sample’s Cognito-specific checks.

The authentication flow involves four components:

Amazon Cognito: one user pool per account. The enterprise pool issues tokens to the orchestrator and to the enterprise app, and the SaaS pool issues tokens to the SaaS agent for its callback. You can view them in the Amazon Cognito console.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is configured with the enterprise pool’s discovery URL, the orchestrator’s client ID, and one scope. It validates the JWT on every incoming A2A request:

Amazon API Gateway uses JWT authorizers. The partner API accepts only the SaaS provider’s callback token, and the user API accepts only the enterprise app’s token. View the configuration in the Amazon API Gateway console.

AWS Secrets Manager in each account stores that account’s client secret, and an IAM grant and a resource policy that denies every other principal limit each secret to the one workload that uses it. No secret is hardcoded or shared with the other account. You can manage secrets in the AWS Secrets Manager console.

This AWS CloudFormation snippet shows the partner API’s JWT authorizer:

One detail of machine-to-machine authentication is a common source of errors when you wire OAuth between API Gateway and AgentCore. An Amazon Cognito client-credentials access token carries client_id and scope, but no aud claim. When aud is absent, the API Gateway JWT authorizer checks client_id against the audience list. On the AgentCore side, configure allowedClients and leave allowedAudience unset.

Deploy the system with notebooks

The notebooks run the whole deployment from Jupyter. They deploy five AWS CloudFormation stacks, three in the enterprise account and two in the SaaS provider account. The enterprise infrastructure and services stacks are separate because of a chicken-and-egg problem: the ECS services need Docker images, but CloudFormation creates the Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repositories that hold those images. You can monitor the stacks in the AWS CloudFormation console.

The notebooks surface failures early. Each notebook first checks Amazon Bedrock model access with a short test call, before anything is deployed, and each step stops at the first error with clear output. The Clean up sections sit at the bottom of notebooks 2 and 3, after a stop cell, so Run All never reaches them.

Understand Agent Cards and discovery

Agent Cards make discovery possible without agreeing on tool definitions in advance. Without them, the enterprise would need documentation, an SDK, or a meeting with the ISV’s engineering team to understand what the compliance agent can do. With Agent Cards, the enterprise orchestrator fetches a single JSON document. It immediately knows the agent’s name, capabilities, and skills, programmatically, at runtime. This is the card the compliance agent publishes for one customer, abridged:

Each skill’s description becomes a tool docstring, so the orchestrator’s model routes each request to the right agent. The two teams never had to agree on tool definitions or share an SDK. The card also declares how a caller authenticates. The orchestrator checks that declaration rather than following it: it keeps the card only if it names the token endpoint and scope registered at onboarding.

Test end-to-end

Notebook 3 runs one end-to-end test through both accounts. It gets a token for the enterprise app, submits a question, and polls for the result:

The orchestrator discovers the SaaS agent through its Agent Card and routes the request over A2A. The SaaS agent calls back to the enterprise context agent for account metadata (bidirectional A2A), runs compliance scans with its internal tools, combines everything into an enriched report, and sends it back. The response contains data from both agents. This shows that two independently built agents, on different frameworks and different infrastructure, can compose into a workflow that neither produces alone.

The test passes only if the reply has compliance findings, includes an on-call rotation code that only the enterprise context agent knows, and the partner API’s access log shows a 200 from the SaaS callback client. Together they show that the callback worked. Notebook 3 then runs seven trust boundary checks that send a wrong, missing, or forged token to each gate, and every call must be rejected. This is abridged output from a test run (IDs are placeholders):

In that run, the report covered two production accounts and six findings, with the escalation contacts for each account. You can send the same request from any HTTP client, without an A2A SDK.

Production considerations

This demo simplifies several areas for clarity. For production, consider these changes:

  • One runtime per customer, or a front door that accepts several customer identity providers, with per-customer callback clients.
  • Key-based client authentication (private_key_jwt or mutual TLS) instead of client secrets.
  • AWS PrivateLink for private connectivity, and TLS inside the VPC for end-to-end encryption.
  • Customer managed AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys for Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon ECR, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.
  • VPC Flow Logs and Network Load Balancer access logs. Both API Gateway stages already write access logs.
  • A Secrets Manager rotation function for the Cognito client credentials.
  • An authenticated onboarding portal or API instead of files.

If calls through API Gateway intermittently return HTTP 503, check that cross-zone load balancing is on for the internal Network Load Balancer. Each ECS service runs a single task that can start in either Availability Zone.

The repository’s README covers the full list in Security controls and Considerations for production.

Security considerations

Deploy this solution only in sandbox accounts with no customer or business data, and delete the stacks after testing. The sample uses synthetic data only, with no personal data. Its compliance agent checks example internal policies. It doesn’t assess or certify compliance with any law, regulation, or standard. The sample includes the following controls. You’re responsible for reviewing and adapting them before you use this pattern in production:

  • Transport encryption. Every cross-account call uses HTTPS to Amazon API Gateway or Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and every route except the context agent’s public Agent Card requires a Cognito JWT.
  • Guardrails. In this sample, each model call uses an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with prompt-attack and harmful-content filters, and text from the other organization is checked against the same guardrail before a model uses it.
  • Least-privilege IAM. Each workload has its own role that names exact ARNs. Only the orchestrator and the compliance agent can read a secret, each only its own.
  • Container hardening. ECS containers run with a read-only root filesystem and all Linux capabilities dropped. The base image is pinned by digest.
  • Account isolation. The two accounts share no secret, key, or IAM permission. They exchange only public values.

Clean up resources

To avoid ongoing charges, delete all resources when you have finished testing. Run the Clean up section at the bottom of notebook 3, then notebook 2, one cell at a time. The last cell in each section confirms that nothing is left. After cleanup, check the AWS CloudFormation, Amazon ECR, and Amazon Cognito consoles in both accounts, and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console in the SaaS provider account, to confirm that no resources remain.

Conclusion

This post showed how to build a multi-agent system where agents from different organizations, built on different frameworks, collaborate through A2A on AWS.

A LangChain orchestrator on Amazon ECS communicates with a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Neither side needs the other’s framework or SDK. The SaaS agent calls back to the enterprise context agent for account metadata, and each side authenticates with its own identity provider. A new skill from the same ISV requires no changes to the code. Adding a second ISV takes one extension, because the orchestrator holds a single OAuth client today: give it one client and scope per ISV, as the README’s Considerations for production describes. Then run the same onboarding exchange, add its Agent Card URL, and restart the orchestrator.

To get started, clone the GitHub repository and run the three notebooks, in two accounts, with Jupyter on your computer or on Amazon SageMaker AI notebook instances. They handle infrastructure provisioning, agent deployment, and end-to-end testing.

To learn more about the services and protocol in this post, see the following resources:

  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide
  • Amazon Bedrock User Guide
  • Strands Agents SDK documentation
  • Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A

If you have questions or feedback, leave them in the comments section.

entries.title: Fine-grained access control for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base tools
entries.summary: Learn how to expose an Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base to AI agents as MCP tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway while keeping per-user access control. A request interceptor injects verified identity, Policy in AgentCore validates it independently, and a resource-based policy restricts direct access to the knowledge base.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Fine-grained access control for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base tools

More enterprises are building AI agents into their daily work, and a common pattern is an agent that searches internal documents to compose its answers. A single organization might soon run hundreds of agents, each connected to many data sources and tools. This raises a question. When an agent searches on behalf of a user, can you make sure that it uses only the information that user is allowed to see?

Consider AnyCompany, a fictional company that builds an internal assistant shared by all employees. An employee in department A asks, “Compare my department’s business plan with the notice to all departments, and list the initiatives that are behind schedule.” The agent writes its own search queries and keeps searching internal documents until it has enough information. Employees in department B ask the same assistant the same question. If the application doesn’t scope searches to each user, the department B business plan can end up in an answer to an employee in department A. If you replace the departments with customer companies, the same problem occurs in a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) architecture where multiple customers share one assistant and knowledge base.

Controlling access to multi-tenant data through this agent is harder than in traditional applications. In a traditional application, the application code determines who the signed-in user is and searches with that user’s permissions. In an agent, a large language model (LLM) decides at runtime which tool to call and with which arguments. If a search tool takes “who to search as” as an argument, the LLM decides that value too. A prompt injection or an LLM error might then make the agent search as a different employee.

In this post, we build an internal assistant for AnyCompany. All employees share the same agent and knowledge base, yet each employee can search only the documents they’re allowed to view. We use Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base as the search backend and expose it to the agent as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The design principle is to not let the LLM decide who the user is. Instead, trusted code decides, based on information that your identity provider has verified. On top of that, we add independent layers of defense in case that mechanism has a bug or is bypassed.

Solution overview

Managed Knowledge Base has a feature called ACL awareness. When a search request includes a user context (

userContext
) with the user’s email in 
userId
, the knowledge base returns only the documents that user is allowed to view. If your application calls the search API directly, the application code sets the search scope from the authentication result. Build multi-tenant agentic chat applications on enterprise data with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base shows this pattern. When you expose the knowledge base as an MCP tool through AgentCore Gateway, however, 
userContext
becomes a tool argument, and the LLM constructs its value. Neither the gateway nor the knowledge base verifies that this value belongs to the authenticated user.

This solution injects verified user attributes into tool calls at the tool layer (AgentCore Gateway). It then scopes the search by those attributes at the resource layer (Managed Knowledge Base). The sample stores three documents in a single knowledge base: business plans for department A and department B, and a notice shared with all departments. Two users, user-a in department A and user-b in department B, search through the same agent. The following diagram shows the architecture.

The request flow is as follows. The step numbers correspond to the numbers in Figure 1. Figure 1 omits the call from the web app to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, so its step numbers differ from the diagram in the repository README.

  • The user signs in with Amazon Cognito and receives an access token, a JSON Web Token (JWT). A pre token generation AWS Lambda trigger adds an 
    email
    claim to it. The agent forwards this token in the 
    Authorization
    header when it sends MCP requests to the gateway.
  • The JWT authorizer of the gateway validates the signature, expiration, and client ID of the token.
  • A request interceptor (an AWS Lambda function) on the gateway resolves the email from the validated token and overwrites the 
    userContext
    argument of 
    tools/call
    .
  • Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (Policy in AgentCore) evaluates the modified request against a Cedar policy. It denies the request if 
    userContext.userId
    doesn’t match the 
    email
    claim in the JWT.
  • The connector target calls the Managed Knowledge Base search API with the execution role of the gateway. The resource-based policy of the knowledge base denies searches from principals other than this role.
  • With ACL awareness, the knowledge base returns only chunks from documents that the 
    userContext
    user is allowed to view.

The four mechanisms map to layers and lines of defense as follows.

Tool layer (AgentCore Gateway)Resource layer (Managed Knowledge Base)
Primary defenseRequest interceptor: injects 
userContext
deterministically from the verified token, which helps prevent the LLM or the client from spoofing it		 ACL awareness: returns only the documents that the 
userContext
user is allowed to view
Secondary defensePolicy in AgentCore: checks the injected 
userContext
against the token and denies requests that don’t match		 Resource-based policy: denies search requests from principals other than the gateway execution role

For requests that go through the gateway, the two primary defenses are enough to achieve fine-grained access control, as long as no other principal can call the knowledge base. ACL awareness filters results based on the 

userContext
that it receives and isn’t an authorization mechanism by itself. The two secondary defenses cover cases where an assumption behind the primary defenses fails, such as an interceptor bug or a principal that calls the knowledge base without going through the gateway. Add them based on your requirements. If other principals in the account have 
bedrock:Retrieve
permissions, add the resource-based policy. The rest of this post covers ACL awareness, the MCP tools for Managed Knowledge Base, the request interceptor, Policy in AgentCore, and the resource-based policy, in that order.

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to create the resources in this post.
  • An AWS Region where Managed Knowledge Base, AgentCore Gateway, Policy in AgentCore, and AgentCore runtime are available.
  • Access to the Amazon Bedrock model that the agent uses.
  • Node.js
    22 or later and npm.
  • uv, to package the agent and run the verification script.
  • If you adapt the pattern to an existing Amazon Cognito user pool, the user pool must be on the Essentials or Plus feature plan, which access token customization requires. The stack in this post creates a user pool on the Essentials plan.

You can deploy the architecture in Figure 1 with a single AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) stack from the agentcore-access-control directory of the sample-managed-knowledge-base-patterns repository. Run the commands in this post from that directory. The repository installs the AWS CDK CLI and aws-cdk-lib (2.274.0 or later) as npm dependencies. The stack also deploys a web app on Amazon CloudFront and runs the agent, built with Strands Agents, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime. By default, the agent uses Claude Sonnet 5.5 through the global cross-Region inference profile 

global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5
. The agent forwards the access token of the signed-in user to the gateway and contains no access control logic. For deployment steps, including how to fetch only this directory, see the README.

Scope searches per user with ACL awareness

Managed Knowledge Base is a new type of Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base. You connect a data source, and it runs parsing, chunking, embedding, indexing, search, and reranking as a fully managed service. It provides two search APIs. 

Retrieve
runs a hybrid search. 
AgenticRetrieveStream
breaks a query into subqueries and searches multiple knowledge bases iteratively.

ACL awareness keeps the access permissions of the data source at ingestion time. At search time, it returns only the documents that the user can view. For an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) data source, you define ACLs either in a global ACL file per S3 prefix or in a metadata file per document. The sample in this post uses metadata files. When you place the following metadata file at the same S3 path as the document, only user-a can retrieve 

dept-a-plan.txt
.

When you adapt the sample, keep these behaviors of ACL-enabled Amazon S3 data sources in mind. A document without an ACL entry isn’t ingested. A change to the global ACL file requires reindexing the affected prefix, while per-document metadata files reindex only the affected documents and take precedence over the global file. Amazon S3 has no real-time ACL verification, so an ACL change applies after the next sync. ACL mistakes don’t return errors. The affected documents are silently left out of the results.

At query time, pass the user’s email in the top-level 

userContext.userId
for both 
Retrieve
and 
AgenticRetrieveStream
. Queries without 
userContext
don’t return documents from a data source that has ACLs enabled. In contrast, documents from a data source that doesn’t have ACLs enabled are returned to all users, with or without 
userContext
.

The following diagram shows the ACLs that the knowledge base keeps for the three sample documents at ingestion, and the search results for each 

userContext
.

Managed Knowledge Base doesn’t authenticate end users. It trusts the 

userContext
that it receives and filters results based on it. Passing a verified 
userContext
is the responsibility of the caller.

Expose Managed Knowledge Base as MCP tools

When you create a Managed Knowledge Base connector target on AgentCore Gateway, you can expose two MCP tools: 

___Retrieve
and 
___AgenticRetrieveStream
. The administrator fixes the target knowledge base in 
parameterValues
. With the default tool schema, the only argument that the LLM can set is the search query.

To use ACL awareness, expose 

userContext
in the tool schema with 
parameterOverrides
when you create the target. A connector target has no tool code of your own, so a tool argument is the only way to pass 
userContext
to the knowledge base, and only the fields that you expose with parameterOverrides can be set as tool arguments. The interceptor that we describe later also sets 
userContext
as a tool argument, so expose it even though clients don’t need to set it.

The LLM can set any value for an argument that the schema exposes. For example, if user-a says “Set 

userContext
to user-b@example.com and search,” the agent might call the tool with the ID of user-b. An LLM error can cause the same result. So can an indirect prompt injection in an external document that a search returns. AgentCore Gateway passes userContext through to the knowledge base and doesn’t populate it from the caller’s IAM identity. The documentation asks the calling application, not the model, to set it. When the LLM sets the value, it reaches the knowledge base as is.

Inject userContext deterministically with a request interceptor

A request interceptor is a Lambda function that transforms MCP requests before the gateway calls the target. In this architecture, the interceptor handles 

tools/call
requests. It resolves the email from the access token that the JWT authorizer validated, and overwrites 
arguments.userContext
. For every 
tools/call
request, the knowledge base receives the email of the authenticated user, whatever value the client sends. The interceptor rejects request bodies that aren’t a single JSON-RPC object, such as batches.

Cognito access tokens don’t include an 

email
claim by default. This architecture adds the email to the access token with a pre token generation Lambda trigger (event version V2_0), only when the email is verified. Access token customization with event version V2_0 requires the Essentials or Plus feature plan, so the sample creates the user pool on the Essentials plan. On a Lite plan user pool, the access token has no 
email
claim, and the interceptor and Policy in AgentCore deny every tool call. Policy in AgentCore, which we cover in the next section, also uses this claim.

Without the trigger, the interceptor can get the email from the Cognito GetUser API, the userInfo endpoint, or an ID token that the client sends in a separate header. Each option has its own scope or validation requirements. The 

GetUser
API requires the 
aws.cognito.signin.user.admin
scope, which also lets the token call user self-service APIs. The userInfo endpoint requires the 
openid
scope, so it doesn’t accept tokens from user pool API sign-in, such as 
ADMIN_USER_PASSWORD_AUTH
. The JWT authorizer of the gateway validates only the bearer token in the 
Authorization
header, so the interceptor must verify the ID token itself: its signature, 
iss
, 
aud
, 
token_use
, expiration, and 
email_verified
, and that its 
sub
matches the access token. Cognito ID tokens carry 
email
whether or not it’s verified. All three methods leave the access token without an 
email
