claim. The policy in the next section then has nothing to compare with and denies every call, so use these methods only if you don’t add Policy in AgentCore.

With another identity provider (IdP), such as Microsoft Entra ID, you can add 

email
to access tokens as an optional claim for both defenses to reference. However, Microsoft doesn’t guarantee that this value is correct or immutable and advises against using it for authorization. For ACL matching, your IdP or application must verify the association between the authenticated user and their email within trusted tenants. Update ACLs and sync the data source when email addresses change or are reassigned.

ACL matching uses an exact email match, so your identity provider must keep each email unique and unchanged. For this reason, the sample user pool disables self sign-up and makes the email attribute immutable.

You attach the interceptor in 

interceptorConfigurations
of the gateway. With 
passRequestHeaders: true
, the gateway passes the 
Authorization
header that the JWT authorizer validated to the interceptor. The headers that the gateway passes include the bearer token, so make sure that the interceptor doesn’t log them. The sample logs only the tool name, whether the client supplied 
userContext
, and whether the interceptor replaced it, not the event, the headers, or the token.

Cognito access tokens carry the app client ID in 

client_id
and include 
aud
only when the client requests resource binding. The JWT authorizer checks allowedClients against client_id and allowedAudience against aud, and verifies both when you set both. So set only 
allowedClients
to the app client ID. With resource binding, you can also set 
allowedAudience
to the resource URI in 
aud
.

The MCP client only attaches the access token to the 

Authorization
header. It doesn’t need code that handles 
userContext
. In the sample, the agent on AgentCore runtime forwards the access token that it received from the web app.

In the sample, AgentCore runtime and the gateway accept the same access token, and the agent forwards it. If your requirements call for tokens that only one resource accepts, request them with resource binding and set 

allowedAudience
on each authorizer. Resource binding is available only with managed login.

Validate the injected request with Policy in AgentCore

With only the interceptor, access control depends on a single component. In the following cases, the gateway accepts a request with an invalid 

userContext
as is:
  • A bug in the interceptor injects a wrong value or skips the overwrite.
  • An unauthorized code change injects the value of another user.
  • A configuration change detaches the interceptor from the gateway.

Policy in AgentCore evaluates tool calls to the gateway with Cedar policies. It runs after the request interceptor. It can reference the claims of the token that the JWT authorizer validated as tags on the principal. The following policy permits a call only when the injected 

userContext.userId
matches the 
email
claim in the JWT. The policy engine denies calls that don’t meet this condition.

In this policy, 

principal
represents the authenticated user, and 
resource
specifies the gateway ARN. The action 
kb___Retrieve
refers to the 
Retrieve
tool on the gateway target named 
kb
. The 
when
clause requires the tool argument 
userContext.userId
to match the JWT’s 
email
claim. The snippet shows the policy for 
kb___Retrieve
. The sample creates a second policy with the same condition for 
kb___AgenticRetrieveStream
, because each policy names a single action and the policy engine denies any request that no permit policy matches.

The following figure shows how Policy in AgentCore denies a tool call when the interceptor doesn’t overwrite 

userContext
correctly.

The interceptor and the policy both use the email from the same token, but they read it from different sources. The policy takes the expected value from the signature-verified token, and the actual value from the request body that the interceptor built. This lets it detect a missing interceptor or a wrong injection. The IdP, the pre token generation trigger, and the policy configuration itself remain shared dependencies of both. With the policy alone, the LLM goes back to constructing 

userContext
, so we recommend that you combine injection and validation.

You attach the policy engine that holds the Cedar policy in 

policyEngineConfiguration
of the gateway. When you set 
mode
to 
ENFORCE
, the gateway denies requests based on the evaluation result. When you add policies to a gateway that’s already in use, you can start with 
LOG_ONLY
, check the decisions in the traces, and then switch to 
ENFORCE
.

Create the gateway target before creating the Cedar policies. Creating the target registers its tool schema with the policy engine. Policy creation fails if a policy references a tool that has not yet been registered, whatever the validationMode.

Restrict access to the knowledge base with a resource-based policy

Policy in AgentCore evaluates only requests that go through a gateway with the policy engine attached. Two paths bypass the tool-layer controls. One is another gateway without the interceptor and the policy that points to the same knowledge base. The other is a direct call to the 

Retrieve
API from an SDK or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI).

Managed Knowledge Base supports resource-based policies. When you attach the following policy to the knowledge base, it explicitly denies 

Retrieve
and 
GetDocumentContent
to principals other than the gateway execution role. Agentic retrieval can call 
GetDocumentContent
to expand results to full documents. An explicit deny takes precedence over an allow in an identity-based policy in the same account, so the deny also applies to administrators and to other consumers of the knowledge base, such as the test window on the console. If other roles need to search the knowledge base, add their Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) to 
ArnNotEquals
.

With AWS CDK, you can attach this policy document with 

CfnKnowledgeBasePolicy
, which maps to the 
AWS::Bedrock::KnowledgeBasePolicy
resource type. Set 
aws:PrincipalArn
to the ARN of the gateway execution role, for example 
gwRole.roleArn
.

You can’t list 

bedrock:AgenticRetrieveStream
in the 
Action
element of the policy. However, the searches inside AgenticRetrieveStream authorize bedrock:Retrieve for the caller on each knowledge base. As a result, the deny in this policy also blocks searches through 
AgenticRetrieveStream
.

A resource-based policy limits which IAM principals can search the knowledge base. It can’t deny another gateway that reuses the same execution role. Don’t share the execution role with other workloads. Restrict which users can pass the role (

iam:PassRole
) and manage the resource-based policy (
bedrock:PutResourcePolicy
, 
bedrock:GetResourcePolicy
, and 
bedrock:DeleteResourcePolicy
), because anyone who can change or delete the policy can remove this control. The policy also doesn’t cover control plane operations such as 
GetKnowledgeBase
, so protect the knowledge base configuration with identity-based policies.

Test the solution

The scripts/verify_defenses.py script in the repository signs in as both users and confirms that each mechanism blocks the path that it targets. Each sample document contains a unique code, so the script can tell from a response whether a document was inadvertently disclosed. The script signs in as the demo users with 

ADMIN_USER_PASSWORD_AUTH
. For the AWS permissions that it needs, see docs/verification.md. The agent scenario depends on the model, so the script reports it as inconclusive (
SKIP
) if the agent doesn’t send the spoofed 
userContext
in three turns.

To check Policy in AgentCore and the resource-based policy on their own, deploy the stack with 

-c enableBypassSimulation=true
. This flag adds two test gateways for the same knowledge base. One has no interceptor, and the other has neither an interceptor nor a policy engine. Both run as a test role that the resource-based policy doesn’t exempt. Redeploy without the flag after testing to remove them. The following table shows the results.
ScenarioResultBlocked by
user-a and user-b send the same queryEach user gets only the documents in their ACLACL awareness
user-a calls 
kb___Retrieve
or 
kb___AgenticRetrieveStream
with the 
userContext
of user-b		 Only the documents user-a can view returnRequest interceptor
user-a prompts the agent to set the 
userContext
of user-b		 The agent might set it. If it does, only the documents user-a can view returnRequest interceptor
A client sends the 
userContext
of another user to a gateway without an interceptor		 The gateway denies the tool call with a 
Tool Execution Denied
error		 Policy in AgentCore
A separate gateway with no interceptor, no policy, and its own execution role searches the knowledge baseThe tool returns an error because the knowledge base denies the searchResource-based policy
A user with administrator permissions calls 
Retrieve
directly from an SDK		 
AccessDeniedException
with an explicit deny in a resource-based policy		 Resource-based policy
A user with administrator permissions calls 
AgenticRetrieveStream
directly from an SDK		 The stream fails with a 
dependencyFailedException
that wraps the explicit deny on 
bedrock:Retrieve
 Resource-based policy

When user-a and user-b send the opening question, the answer for user-a draws on the department A business plan and the notice, and the answer for user-b draws on the department B business plan and the notice.

The web app shows the tool arguments that the LLM generated next to the documents that came back. When user-a asks the agent to search as user-b, the app shows the spoofed 

userContext
, but only the documents of user-a appear.

The following screenshot shows the web app after user-a asks the agent to search as user-b.

Clean up

To avoid future charges, delete the stack when you finish testing. Run 

npx cdk destroy
in the 
infra
directory of the pattern. This deletes the knowledge base, the S3 buckets and their objects, the user pool, the demo user password in AWS Secrets Manager, and the Amazon CloudWatch Logs log groups of every Lambda function and of the agent runtime.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to share an agent and a knowledge base across a company and still limit each user’s searches to the documents they’re allowed to view. As the primary defense, a request interceptor injects 

userContext
from the verified token, and ACL awareness in Managed Knowledge Base scopes the search. Based on your requirements, Policy in AgentCore validates the injected value independently, and a resource-based policy denies searches that bypass the gateway.

The underlying design principle is to not let the LLM generate values that affect authorization. This principle also applies to a multi-tenant SaaS architecture where multiple customers share a knowledge base. It also applies to MCP tools other than Managed Knowledge Base that take arguments affecting access control. Deploy the CDK stack from the GitHub repository and try it with your own data sources and IdP. To learn when to use interceptors and when to use policies, see Secure AI agents with Policy and Lambda interceptors in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway.

The architecture in this post uses the built-in AgentCore Gateway connector for Managed Knowledge Base. If you’re considering migrating from a Customer-managed Knowledge Base to a Managed Knowledge Base, the 

amazon-bedrock
skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS includes a migration procedure to help you evaluate and plan the transition. It works in coding agents that you already use, such as Kiro, Claude Code, and Cursor. The agent reads your current configuration with read-only calls and writes a migration plan, optionally with a cost comparison based on your measured usage. After you approve the plan, it creates the new knowledge base next to the original and doesn’t change or delete the original. For the benefits of Managed Knowledge Base and a step-by-step migration walkthrough, see Migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with your coding agent.
